security, privacy, and ethical issues are a primary concern for stakeholders and evidence of the need for adequate policies to leverage big data tools (Kamilaris et al., 2017; Rotz et al., 2019). It is also necessary to develop appropriate incentives to create bi-directional data-output sharing relationships between farmers, especially smallholders, and private ventures (WEF, 2012; Zhang et al., 2021), thus providing value-added alternatives to producers. Generating relationships of trust between and in the big data solutions and agricultural actors as such. Moreover, access to these solutions and the interpretation of their results remain a major constraint to overcome.

One solution does not ﬁt all, as there are a multitude of alternatives that are already addressing some of the above- mentioned issues. In this article, Crop Observatories are presented as one of these alternatives, with the aim to guide the decision- making process around speciﬁc crops and the needs of diﬀerent types of stakeholders in these value chains. They also aim to address the issue of access to reliable data, which remains a constraint for many smallholder farmers. Moreover, while many digital solutions have proven to be successful and have a positive impact on smallholder farmers in developing countries, there is an over-concentration of these solutions in a handful of selected countries (Porciello et al., 2021), whereas Observatories have a broader scope by not only having a global reach, but also by presenting the importance of contextualizing a user’s reality in relation to the rest of the world. In addition, Observatories respond to the need to synthesize information by integrating data sources and making it not only more accessible, but also more understandable to a wider audience. While the potential of platforms among impactful digital solutions remains limited, as does the reach of big data products and their beneﬁts to small producers, there is great growth in digital coverage and services in the developing world (Trendov et al., 2019), representing a great potential to drive these innovations and ensure that the most vulnerable are not left behind in this revolution.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Crop Observatories Structure and Data

These Observatories were established from a demand-driven request to provide relevant indicators for speciﬁc crops, with the initial intention to guide scientists and disseminate the scientiﬁc knowledge gathered by the Alliance Bioversity-CIAT. Nonetheless, their scope grew continuously by adding new modules and components of interest to other stakeholders (e.g., policymakers, smallholder and large farmers, intermediaries, industry, and consumers) that demand and beneﬁt from more speciﬁc and data-driven information. The main objectives of the Observatories are to (i) merge and manage diverse open- access datasets that disaggregate relevant indicators to lower administrative units, and contextualize the economic importance of the crop regionally and nationally; (ii) combine and display speciﬁc datasets from multiple research areas (i.e., gene banks, breeding programs, socioeconomic units, food quality and sensory laboratories) under standardized ontologies for analysis; and (iii) link and share this information with an extensive network of partners related to the crops of interest for the

Introduction

Southern Africa countries face significant food security challenges in varying magnitudes. Food insecurity in the region is high and caused by various factors, among them recurrent climate shocks that lead to acute food shortages among low-income families. Besides, the region’s eco- nomic challenges and the novel COVID 19 pandemic and the subsequent containment measures, have further reduced access to diverse food varieties (Nchanji et al., 2021a). As a result, cases of malnu- trition have increased in the region. Zimbabwe is one of the Southern Africa country with the highest numbers of food-insecure people (Nchanji and Mutari, 2019). The country has reported some of the worst food security cases: Nearly half of its population face the risk of starvation (Relief Web, 2021). The on-going pandemic is exacerbating the already dire food security situation for both rural and ur- ban populations. For instance, loss of income among urban and peri-urban inhabitants has subjected them to increased poverty, creating difficulties in obtaining sufficient food due to low purchasing power. A majority of informal and formal businesses have either shut down during the pandemic or continue to operate at minimal levels (Nchanji and Lutomia, 2021), with shocks transmitted to rural households through reduced remittances and reduced access to markets. These have reduced incomes for smallholder farmers which has implications on crop production and food consumption.

Common bean is an important food crop that can address some of the food security challenges in Zimbabwe. The crop is adapted to varied agronomic and climatic conditions and is suitable for small- scale farmers with limited resources. It can thrive under limited input use and can be intercropped with other cash crops. The crop is an important source of dietary protein. It is rich in starch, dietary fiber, and several minerals, including iron, zinc, thiamine, vitamin B6, and potassium which are es- sential in addressing high levels of malnutrition in Zimbabwe. Besides its nutrient composition, com- mon bean is also widely grown in the country and is essential for people of all income categories (Katungi et al., 2020). Women are primarily responsible for its production hence emphasizing its role in turnaround of fortunes of vulnerable groups of people and households (Nchanji et al., 2021b) Furthermore, small-scale farmers have access to different common bean varieties that can be grown in different climatic conditions.

The crop is grown throughout the year when weather changes are not severe because it takes a short- er time to mature. It is popular among small-scale farmers and is considered a staple food in most households. Through increased yield and productivity, bean farmers have significantly increased the per capita bean consumption. Katungi et al. (2020) posits that through financial support from insti- tutions such as the Global Affairs Canada and Swiss Agency for Development Cooperation (SDC), bean production in Zimbabwe has shown significant improvement. These flagship interventions have enhanced production by increasing access to quality seeds and farmer training. The distance between a farmer and the nearest seed dealer fell by nearly 60 percent, significantly increasing access to seeds as the distance reduced from 25 kilometres to 10 kilometres. The demand for certified seeds also increased by nearly 3 kilograms per producer (Katungi et al., 2020). Additionally, the adoption of improved bean varieties enhanced bean production.

Plant breeding is important to food security because it contributes to higher crop yields and offers considerable potential for sustainable agricultural development and food security. A significant pro- portion of Zimbabwe’s population is chronically hungry and could benefit from plant breeding tech- nologies to avert the challenges associated with malnutrition, such as impaired mental and physical development. Growing food for the ever-increasing population is a challenge in the contemporary world (Qaim, 2020). Therefore, plant breeding is important because it enhances crop resilience to

Gender is an integral part of bean breeding initiatives and provides the platform through which plant breeding should be implemented. Gender-sensitive breeding offers a clear focus on addressing gender gap in agriculture by considering different traits preferred by both men and women (Nchanji et al., 2021b). Through the gender lens, critical elements in women and men’s preferences are consulted even though such profiles do not necessarily have different traits for men and women (Nchanji et al., 2021b). Breeding teams are therefore capable of assessing gender-relevant differences in preferences, constraints, needs, and potential impact on women and men’s livelihood strategies. This observation is founded on the critical role women play in production of common beans in Zimbabwe. Therefore, their participation in bean breeding initiatives is considered essential because it is regarded as a wom- en’s crop (PABRA 2015a). Mechanization initiatives that target bean production consider women’s preferences, such as using threshers to reduce drudgery and Purdue Improved Crop Storage (PICS) bags and solar bubble driers to reduce post-harvest losses.

Bean breeding in Zimbabwe has relatively improved and earned the country research reputation. The country’s long-established agricultural research system has enabled it to make significant steps in gender-sensitive breeding initiative. Zimbabwe has managed to assess and cover all essential and high priority traits in the common bean through its national breeding programs. The country has forged collaborative private and public linkages to strengthen its national breeding program. The bean breeding situation in Zimbabwe has improved and taken a demand-driven approach to indentify gaps and propose possible practical solutions. The breeding activities were developed using the informa- tion collected during participatory varietal selection and other meetings. The integration of gender aspects in the breeding activities has since proved important for breeding pipelines.

The CGIAR gender and breeding initiative has developed an important tool to guide breeders in identifying the gender gaps and preferences of customer to develop and prioritize new product that address persistent gender gaps in crop production. The tool; G+ product and customer profile recog- nizes changes in the modern agriculture as production and marketing systems transition towards more demand-driven business models for social inclusivity. The G+ approach in bean breeding offers a well-integrated and evidence-based protocol for common bean breeding. With the G+ customer profiles, bean breeding creates the type of crops that customers need (Orr et al., 2018; CGIAR, n. d.). The approach is essential in characterizing targeted groups with new varieties by considering gender differences in knowledge to make it easier to develop the right product for the right customers.

Therefore, this report applies the G+ tools to the common bean value chain in Zimbabwe by providing information that updates the product profile. This is achieved through literature review, survey data and existing participatory varietal selection. In this regard, the information herein is supposed to guide the breeding programs as they strategize and transition to developing socially inclusive products. The report also aims to document and provide critical information for updating the G+ tool because it is still work in progress. Furthermore, it provides summarized market segment information for an end-to-end development of product profiles in Zimbabwe. In doing so, the reports document existing gaps, progress notwithstanding, that can inform development of new product profiles. To present this information, the report is divided into three sections: customer profiling, product profiling, and gaps.

1.1 Product Mapping

In Zimbabwe, common bean is a staple food and is preferred by households across the various social classes in the country. Therefore, it is an important food crop to enhance the country’s food security. The food crop is consumed in both rural and urban areas of Zimbabwe where it complements other foodstuffs. Dry beans remain the most valuable product traded in most of Zimbabwe’s open-air mar- kets. Dry beans are cheaper to store and transport. Unlike dry beans, fresh bean supply is limited be- cause it is seasonal and therefore not readily available in the market. Self-employed men and women are the primary producers of common beans. They rely on rain-fed and irrigation, and often have to deal with poorly functioning markets (FAO, n. d.). Nevertheless, the common bean is a preferred crop in rural areas because of its income potential.

The crop is produced under six farming systems. Communal land farming system is the most domi- nant system accounting for about 37 percent of the total bean output in Zimbabwe as from 2015. The A1 farms system, which are large-scale commercial farms (demarcated village) account for about

Other bean farming systems are old resettlement, small-scale commercial, and large-scale commercial. Due to agro-ecological di- versity in Zimbabwe, bean production is carried out in most regions, include Mashonaland, Midlands, Manicaland, Matabeleland, and Masvingo.
1.1.1 Bean Products for Food Security

Bean products available in Zimbabwe for consumption include canned beans, flour, bean snacks, and pre-cooked beans. Frozen beans and canned beans are not common among the rural popula- tion because of their high prices and refrigeration requirements: making them out of reach for most households. Therefore, most preparation method used is cooking which requires a lot of time, fuel, and water. Achieving food security requires the development of affordable and convenient on-the- shelf bean products that need less fuel cost, time, and water for cooking. This approach will enhance bean consumption in the country and improve the welfare of a significant number of the country’s population because nearly 70 percent of its population are rural farmers (FAO, n. d). Precooked bean products are the most common bean product that is relatively affordable in the country. The three categories of pre-cooked bean products include, ready to eat bean snack, bean flour, and a pre-cooked bean that takes a shorter time to cook.
1.1.2 Processed Bean Products

Bean powders and flour are the most common and most outstanding innovations in the bean world. Bean powder is commonly used in boosting protein levels in various recipes. Bean flour provides essential qualities that include water retention, gelation, adhesion and emulsification. These ingre- dients are essential and can replace other ingredients such as eggs in baked goods. Bean flour is also essential for use in gluten-free bakeries. Bean flours are now produced and consumed across Sub-saharan Africa through the Pan Africa Bean Research Alliance (PABRA) scaling out initiatives. Furthermore, Zimbabwe has canned bean products. Bean-cereal grain composites are also important processed products.
1.1.3 Bio-fortified Bean Products

Common bean has several dietary benefits and assists the local population in addressing nutrition challenges. Through conventional breeding, farmers in Zimbabwe benefit from the production of common beans. The product generates significant income and is popular among local farmers be- cause of its niche market as nutritious food products. The growing demand for the crop represents significant production and consumption quantities of the country’s product. NUA45 and NUA674 are some of the bio-fortified bean varieties for industrial processing (Nchanji et al., 2021b).
1.2 Step 2: Customer Mapping

Common bean is one of the most consumed leguminous crops in the Zimbabwe and Southern Africa. As a multifunctional crop and food, it is widely consumed and recognized by the Zimbabwean gov- ernment as central to achievement of food security in the country (Katungi et al., 2017). It is also a source of income for thousands of households and small business owners.
1.2.1 Actors in the Value Chain

Women play a significant role in common bean production, processing, preserving and marketing. It is considered a women’s crop because of the number of women participating in the crop production. Despite existing difference in Zimbabwe’s various regions, women tend to take the lead in nearly all areas of bean production. Beside bean production, women are also involved in bean trade. Other actors in bean value chain are farm input suppliers, local market traders, aggregators, processors, agricultural extension systems and agents, and consumers.

1.2.3 Processors

Food companies involved in industrial processing of canned bean products of mostly sugar beans and Calima market class, but also started canning NUA45 for its nutritional content and market. The sugar and Calima market classes are preferred for canning because they are small-sized, an important qual- ity parameter for canning varieties (Mutari et al., 2021). Established canning companies among them National Foods, Africa Preserves, Olivine Industries Limited, and Cairns Foods Ltd. There are also small-scale processors in the rural communities made up of women groups such as the Chimanimani women group etc. On the other hand, large-seeded cultivars are preferred by small-scale processors, who are mostly informal businesswomen.

This category of bean value chain actors comprises seed traders, grain traders, and aggregators. Infor- mal seed traders are farmers through exchanges with other fellow farmers, friends, and neighbours, and local or urban market traders who buy, select, sort and clean seed that is mostly sold untreated. These types of seed traders dominate the Zimbabwean bean seed system and mostly owned by wom- en. 1.3.1 Poverty Analyses

The evidence table shows a head-count poverty of 38%. Further evidence shows that Zimbabwe struggles with malnutrition. The most vulnerable groups are women and children. Lukwa et al. Stunting among children under five had accelerated between 2012 and 2016, projections indicating that 760,000 children will be stunted by 2025. A significant majority of the country’s labour force in major urban areas have poor quality employ- ment characterized by low wages and poor working conditions. Furthermore, there is a gender imbal- ance in the country’s formal sector. Women are the most affected as most of them are not employed in the formal sector resulting in a high unemployment rate. In the rural areas, most women have low academic qualifications and therefore cannot find gainful employment. As a result, women in the rural areas remain the primary caregivers of families and therefore adequate engage in specialized bean production such attending training for contractual bean production. As a result, poverty is largely a rural phenomena. For additional information about prevalence of poverty by province and prevalence of extreme poverty refer to annexes 1 and 2 respectively.

Innovation Next Innovation ACTIVE: 2018 to present Even with modern genetic tools, it takes years, and a lot of money, to breed a new crop variety. This effort is wasted if farmers refuse to plant the new variety, and if consumers won t buy it. A new crop variety can be successful if plant breeders create the types of crops that people want, but that entails addressing the needs of a large audience. In the end, it is farmers and consumers (including processors), many of whom are women, who decide the fate of a new variety. The tricky part is getting appropriate feedback from all of them. The G+ approach for gender responsive breeding, developed by CGIAR scientists since 2018, offers an integrated, systematic and evidence-based protocol for breeding new crop varieties. The approach builds on work by the CGIAR Excellence in Breeding (EiB) Platform on the concept of a product profile , which describes the traits that different actors want in a new variety, giving plant breeders a target. The G+ approach complements this with two additional tools. The G+ plus customer profile characterizes client groups targeted for new varieties, considering gender differences in knowledge, assets and decision-making which influence adoption. This makes it easier for breeders to develop the right product for the right customers. The tools are crucial as CGIAR breeding transitions towards a more demand-driven, socially inclusive approach. The G+ product profile query tool guides collection of evidence to prioritize the traits in product profiles by examining both potential positive gender impacts of those traits, but also any negative impacts they might have. These two G+ tools enable breeding programs to meaningfully think through social inclusivity, and especially women s trait preferences and the special circumstances of different contexts, recognizing that one size does not fit all. The idea for the innovation emerged from two gender and breeding workshops in which breeders and experienced social scientists realized that breeding new varieties requires understanding the user preferences of women and men from certain walks of life. Breeders, farmers, and consumers will benefit from understanding the traits that different people want in different crops. Varieties that farmers want to plant, that consumers want to buy, will contribute to poverty alleviation and inclusive development. The tools were developed by the CGIAR Gender and Breeding Initiative (GBI) and are being jointly piloted with the CGIAR Excellence in Breeding Platform (EiB) on a selected set of breeding programs. The tools are crucial as CGIAR breeding transitions towards a more demand-driven, socially inclusive approach. In Nigeria, the main crop is cassava, with many farming households earning part of their income from its production. The adoption rate of new improved cassava varieties by female farmers is relatively low in comparison to male farmers. On the other hand, 90% of the cassava produced in Nigeria is used for processing, a task for which women are almost entirely responsible. To address the incorporation of gender and generally enhance the alignment with end user preferences in new varieties, CGIAR researchers at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) and their partners at Nigeria s National Root Crop Research Institute (NRCRI) are currently using the tools in the product profile development process. Traits can have an important effect on food security, and gender equality In Uganda more than 75% of all farmers grow bananas, the country s staple food. While considered a man s crop, banana is oftentimes managed and used by women. Therefore, traits can have an important effect on food security, and gender equality. After a thorough assessment of banana trait preferences from a gender perspective, the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT is using the G+ tools with the banana breeding program at NARO Uganda to develop and assess banana product profiles that enhance benefits and reduce negative consequences for both men and women. While still in the piloting phase, there are encouraging signs that breeding programs will develop varieties which are more widely adopted, and with more favorable impacts for women and their livelihoods. The concept of Integrated Pest Management (IPM) was introduced sixty years ago to curb the overuse of agricultural pesticides, whereby its simplest version (IPM 1.0) was aiming at reducing the frequency of applications. Gradually, agro- ecological principles, such as biological control and habitat management, were included in IPM 2.0. However, throughout this time, smallholder farmers did not improve their decision- making skills and continue to use hazardous pesticides as their first control option. We are therefore proposing a new paradigm — IPM 3.0 — anchored on 3 pillars: 1) real-time farmer access to decision-making, 2) pest-management options relying on science-driven and nature-based approaches, and 3) the integration of genomic approaches, biopesticides, and habitat- management practices. We are convinced that this new paradigm based on technological advances, involvement of youth, gender-responsiveness, and climate resilience will be a game changer. However, this can only become effective through redeployment of public funding and stronger policy support.

The past sixty years of Integrated Pest Management (IPM) have been well- described and characterized in detail [1••] with the fol- lowing simplified historical perspective of IPM. Accord- ingly, the label IPM 1.0 is attributed to the initial efforts in the 1960s and 1970s for drastically reducing the in- discriminate use of pesticides by introducing the notion of threshold-based intervention derived from scouting. For low-literacy farmers in most developing countries, this was a novel and knowledge-intensive concept, which eventually required the introduction of educational-sup- port systems such as the farmer field school (FFS). FFS became a useful approach to teach farmers basic concepts of agro-ecological principles throughout the cropping season though chemical pesticides remained the mainstay of pest-control interventions [2]

During the last 20 years, in the attempt to further mini- mize the application of chemical pesticides, the IPM approach was broadened by increasing the range of nature-based solutions — often limited to biological control — with improved agro-ecological interventions such as planting companion flower banks and other eco- logical engineering measures to increase the presence and efficacy of biological control agents [3••]. To popularize these fairly complex management approaches involving multitrophic interactions, sometimes across landscapes, the same authors developed successful mass-media cam- paigns using rural radios and TV shows. These efforts were pioneered in Vietnam, and in some instances, pes- ticide applications in rice (Oryza sativa) were reduced by up to 60% [4]. Around the same time, the first versions of the ‘push–pull’ concept were developed for maize (Zea mays) in Kenya to exploit plant volatiles attracting pests to nonhosts at the field border, as well as repelling them by companion plants inside the field [5]. This new, improved version of IPM is considered an important upgrade of the previous IPM 1.0 approach and can hence be tagged as IPM 2.0, although this label had already been used in 2013 in conjunction with plant pathology on a special occasion, the 10th Conference of European Foundation for Plant Pathology [6]. We further consider the agro- ecological crop-protection concept proposed by [1••] as one of the most advanced forms of IPM 2.0.

Pillar #1: what does it take to empower smallholder farmers to make their own
decisions in sustainable pest management?

In most of tropical Africa, farmers’ decision to spray their crops is still either calendar-based or triggered by visual and conspicuous pest-attack symptoms. This practice has led to indiscriminate use of synthetic pesticides, with their adverse side effects on human, animal, and environmental health [7••]. In recent years, this trend has been exacerbated by the perceived impacts of cli- mate disturbances, whereby farmers increase the use of pesticides as an adaptive response to mitigate pest-in- duced yield losses [8•].

During previous versions of IPM, attempts to curb this trend have relied on several farmer- training approaches, of which FFS has been widely practiced in tropical Africa. The FFS approach teaches farmers basic princi- ples of agro-ecosystem analysis, with the ultimate goal to make the farmer recognize pests and their damage symptoms in the field and understand when the damage threshold is attained in order to intervene. However, FFS requires a season-long attendance by farmers and trainers organized in small groups, which is resource- intensive and can only reach a small percentage of farmers [9]. Today, most farmers continue to face 1) the widespread lack of appropriate tools to enable them to take informed decisions, 2) limited access to alternatives to harmful pesticides, compounded by 3) the limited availability of personal protective equipment.

Another frequent obstacle to farmer empowerment in decision-making is the lack of proper identification of pest organisms, particularly the damage-inducing life stages. The invasion of the fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) into Africa provides one of the most flagrant

One of the most recent examples illustrating how such a puzzle was cracked, thanks to long years of international collaboration across continents, is that of the legume pod borer Maruca vitrata. In Africa, this pest has been tacitly regarded as indigenous, and after years of unsuccessful efforts in finding resistance in cowpea, a transgenic ap- proach using the Cry1Ab Bt gene was eventually able to provide efficient control [20]. However, concurrent bio- diversity studies revealed substantially different guilds of hymenopterous parasitoids in Africa and tropical Asia. The lack of specific parasitoids in West Africa was par- ticularly intriguing [21], indicating a potential for redis- tribution of biological control agents [22]. Meanwhile, population genetic studies indicated tropical Asia as the most plausible origin of the pest, thereby calling for an experimental assessment of the Asian biological control candidates in the African context [23]. In-depth biolo- gical studies were then undertaken to assess the host- specificity and maternal factors determining the poten- tial of various biological control candidates, and parti- cularly the braconids Liragathis javana and Phanerotoma syleptae [24]. These two hymenopteran parasitoids have been released experimentally in various countries in West Africa, leading to reductions of the pest population
by up to 86% at pilot-release areas [25]. They are

currently being released in biological control campaigns in Benin, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Niger, and Nigeria. The example of M. vitrata highlights the importance of challenging the pest status of organisms that seem to have only poorly adapted natural enemies in a given agro-ecology. A similar case study is that of biological control efforts against the diamondback moth Plutella xylostella. Host plant and parasitoid-diversity studies in South Africa revealed that P. xylostella might originate from this area [26], and this information has been used in several attempts to introduce biological control agents to other regions. This example has been reviewed in detail [27,28] and has provided the basis for the establishment and successful control of P. xylostella, for example, in eastern and southeastern Kenya (Kitui, Mwingi/Yatta, and Loitokitok areas) [29]. Both examples, however, clearly indicate that biological control alone will not provide a silver-bullet solution, and that it will need to be integrated with other compatible measures as illu- strated in the next section.

The last two decades of genomic approaches in breeding for insect-pest resistance have been mostly characterized by successes and failures in staying ahead of the race with pest organisms becoming resistant to Bt-gene constructs. However, more recent advances using the CRISPR–Cas9 technology present new avenues for improving crop resi- lience to pest attacks [30]. Thereby, the aim of this ap- proach is not solely to improve plant resistance to biotic stresses, but also, for example, to modify plant signaling to attract natural enemies, specific parasitoids, as well as generalist predators [31]. Once these tactics get main- streamed and properly integrated into a functional IPM framework as proposed by [32•], they will certainly con- tribute to optimizing biological control outcomes and re- duce the application of unsuitable pesticides.

In Eastern and Southern Africa, potent biopesticides have been developed by the International Centre of Insect Physiology and Ecology (icipe, Nairobi, Kenya) and are now getting into the hands of farmers, thanks to joint endeavors with an emerging private sector [33•]. The integrability of biopesticides in an IPM framework is defined by their degree of selectivity toward nontarget organisms, but generally they have much fewer negative impacts on beneficial insects (including pollinators) than synthetic pesticides [34]. In West Africa, biopesticides gained momentum some 30 years back with the devel- opment of Green Muscle (based on the en- tomopathogenic fungus Metarhizium acridum) against locusts and grasshoppers, however, this effort could not be sustained owing to the lack of innovative private in- itiatives to support their production and commercializa- tion [35]. More recently in Niger, women cooperatives have initiated the commercial production of a ready-to- use biopesticide made of locally available neem-seed powder, which is packed into a small tissue bag, soaked in water overnight, with the resulting solution sprayed the next day on a range of crops. What is innovative here is not the product per se, but the way it is produced and commercialized, which allows to bypass the lack of up-
take by the more formal private sector.

The third major technological breakthrough comes from renewed efforts to improve the push–pull approach, which were spurred by the invasion of S. frugiperda in East Africa. A first upgrade of the original version was described as climate-smart push–pull by including new and drought-resilient varieties of companion plants [36]. This concept was subsequently validated with success to manage S. frugiperda soon after its appearance in Kenya [37], then tested for its potential for integration in con- servation agriculture [38] and fine-tuned for enhanced scaling and adoption by farmers [39••]. Meanwhile, the mechanisms underlying the regulation of S. frugiperda by

The push–pull approach was also investigated for its contribution to improving soil ecosystem services through their positive effects on soil organic matter [41]. Hence, we can infer that the push–pull concept could be a model for integrating other compatible IPM compo- nents as described above. Meanwhile, the IPM frame- work has been expanded to consider both positive and negative interactions between pest-control approaches and pollinators in a systematic way, becoming a new paradigm of Integrated Pest and Pollinator Management (IPPM). It has been defined as a framework for co- management of ecosystem functions driven by pests, natural enemies, and pollinators [42••]. While push–pull works mainly at the field level, IPPM considers ele- ments of landscape management, aligned with an IPM 3.0 vision, whose ultimate goal would be to design and deploy IPM solutions for whole landscapes [43].
Perspectives
Is IPM 3.0 the right solution to curb the pesticide treadmill in Africa?

Past efforts to involve farmers in decision-making for pest management have only yielded marginal successes, mostly at pilot sites [1••]. Since farmers’ buy-in for IPM 3.0 is essential, we put particular emphasis on farmer education and empowerment as the first and most im- portant pillar for our improved IPM strategy. We have enough evidence that smarter insect-pest management can entirely rely on nature-based solutions if deployed correctly and in the right context (as described above in pillars #2 and #3), reducing or avoiding the need for the use of synthetic pesticides [44•].

How do we transition from current practices to IPM 3.0 We strongly believe our vision for IPM based on tech- nological advances, involvement of youth, gender-re- sponsiveness, and climate resilience will be a game changer. The existing agricultural research and exten- sion capacities alone, particularly with the current public funding levels in Africa, however, will not be able to achieve this transformation on their own. We therefore urge a shift in public funding to focus on the need for increased investments in plant health research instead of insisting in quick wins that can easily be achieved by, for example, scaling projects. Who — and with what kind of means — is going to fill the research pipeline to produce the needed plant health innovations for successful IPM implementation in Africa, to deliver impact in the next 10 years and beyond? We should learn from lessons elsewhere, how to create virtuous feedback loops for a diversified agriculture, instead of falling into pernicious feedback loops as described by [45]. For all this to be achieved, a much stronger policy support as proposed by [44•] will be critical. A first essential policy intervention would be the establishment and operationalization of a regional early warning network to deter and intercept

This will allow to in- tegrate horizon scanning and advanced diagnostics approaches for fine-tuning customized pest-management recommendation at landscape and regional scales.

The successful implementation of IPM 3.0 relies on the increased availability and uptake of alternatives to syn- thetic insecticides such as biopesticides. Therefore, we strongly advocate for an enabling policy framework that should include, among others, clear regulatory directives facilitating the registration and use of biopesticides and harmonizing the process at the regional level to avoid the hassle of having to register the same product in each country. These measures should be flanked by the strict enforcement of current rules regulating the use of che- mical pesticide. Additional efforts should be made at national and regional levels to adhere to minimum pes- ticide-residue levels, by providing the necessary infra- structure for their routine verification through accredited laboratories. This will both satisfy the increasing urban consumer demand for healthy and safe agricultural pro- ducts, while also providing additional incentives for the on-farm use of biopesticides. However, we do recognize these policy changes might take time as they would re- quire prior individual country engagement and en- dorsement.

1. Chiyambi cha malimidwe ansomba potsatira kusintha kwa nyengo

Kusintha kwa nyengo ndi zina zotsatira kwabweretsa anthu ambiri obvutika pachiopsezo, kutentha kwanyengo ndi zochitika pa kusintha kwa nthawi ndi nthawi m’madera ambiri padziko lino lapansi. Kutentha koopsa, chilala, madzi osefukira komanso malimidwe amane sadziwika bwino abvutitsa alimi ndi zokolola zawo, kuopsezanso miyoyo yao. Kwa osulidwa ndi obvutika, unyinji wa anthu, ulimi wansomba ndi njira imodzi yokhazikitsara umoyo wa anthu osawerengedwa ndi anthu obvutika chifukwa chogwapo pamaziko achakudya ndi kukhala wanthanzi. Koma alimi ansomba ambiri m’Zambia apita m’mabvuto chifukwa cha nyengo yosadalirika paulimi wokhazikika wansomba.

M’Zambia, madera a kumpoto ndi a ku Luapula, mwacitsanzo, ulimi wansomba ndi usodzi umakhudzidwa chifukwa chanyengo yowopsa, monga madzi osefukira, kutentha kwambiri komanso kagwedwe ka mvula kosadziwika bwino (Unduna umene Umayang’anira zachitukuko 2017). Kasinthidwe kanyengo yowopsa kwabweretsa bvuto lamakhazikidwe yachakudya ndi khalidwe lamadzi, ubwino wa madzi, ndiponso miyoyo ya anthu, makamaka m’madera akumidzi amene amadalira pa chakudya chimene chichokera kumadzi. Ndicodziwika kuti anthu osauka amakhudzidwa kwambiri ngati kutentha kwapita patsogolo, ndipo madera a kumpoto [Northern] ndi a ku Luapula ndiwo madera osauka kwambiri muno m’Zambia, komwe chigawo cha anthu cha 80.5% m’madera awiriwa akuchulidwa kuti ndi osauka ndipo chigawo cha 64.5% ndi osauka kwambiri m’chaka cha 2010 [CSO 2010] Dera la Kummwera kwa Zambia [Southern], limachedwa kuti ndi malo omwe kasinthidwe ka nyengo ndi kosintha kwambiri. Kupitirira kwa zaka makumi yatatu, kwakhala kosagwa mvula bwino ndipo kudzapitirirabe kukumana kwambiri ndi chilala ndiponso madzi osefukira dziko lonse, chimene chidzakhudza mbali yaulimi wansomba ndi wa ziweto (Kalantary 2010).

Chifukwa zachitika ndiponso kukwera kwa nyengo kukuyembekezeka mtsogolo, zoipa zokhudzana ndi umoyo wa anthu, maziko a chakudya, chakudya chopatsa thanzi ndi kusowa thandizo landalama kungapitirire ngati sipadzapezeka njira zochepetsera mwamsangamsanga kuti zikhazikitsidwe. Motero, ndikofunikira kugwirizana ndi alimi, kupeza njira zamalimidwe amakono kupereka uthenga wazanyengo ndi mmmene tingapewere. Njira zimenezi zidzathandizira alimi kuwonjezera momwe angapewere ndikukhala okonzekera pa kusintha kwa nyengo.
1.1 Njira zimene zichepetsa kukhala okonzekera pakusintha kwa nyengo pakati pa alimi ansomba ang’ono-ang’ono.
Njira zimene zibweretsa kusakhala okonzekera kusintha kwa nyengo kuli alimi ndi usodzi: • Kusowekera kwa nsomba zabwino zomwe ndi zolimba kulingana ndi nyengo.
• Kusowekera kwa chakudya chopatsa thanzi chomwe chipezeka m’dziko lathu.
• Kagwiritsidwe koipa kamadzi pakati pa alimi.
• Kusowekera kwa luso pakayendetsedwe kaulimi wansomba wamene upereka patsogolo kukonzekera pakusintha kwanyengo.
• Kusowekera kudziwa mmene nyengo idzakhalira kuti agwiritse nchito alimi ansomba popanga maganizo oyenera.
• Posagwiritsa nchito bwino njira zaulimi wansomba potsatira kusintha kwanyengo kumene • kumapangitsa kukolola ndi kukonzekera.
• Kuchepekera kwa owaphunzitsa pa zomwe iwo amachita kuti alimi akhale aluso ndi nzeru.
• Kusowekera kwa zinthu ndiponso ndi mau ophunzitsira ofunikira kuti anthu akhale okonzekera pa zotsatira za kusintha kwa nyengo.

M’Zambia, kuwonjezera kudziwa pa kugwiritsidwe ka njira zamakono pakasinthidwe kanyengo pa ulimi wa nsomba kungabweretse kukhala ndi chakudya chokwanira ndi kudzetsa umoyo wabwino kwa alimi ang’ono-ang’ono ansomba. Kulingana ndi kusintha kwanyengo, tsono, ili buku lidzapangitsa kupeza njira zomwe kukhala okonzekera panjira zamakono kuli alimi angono-angono ndi ena onse okhudzidwa mmene angapezere uphungu kukhala okonzekera
Malimidwe okonzekera ndi olimba panyengo paulimi wansomba: e Kugwirizanitsa ulimi wansomba ndi ulimi waziweto zing’ono-zing’ono

ndi luso la zamakono m’chakudya chansomba. Buku ili ndi ndondomeko yothandizira aphunzitsi pophunzitsa alimi ang’ono-ang’ono pa zomwe afunikira kudziwa pakasinthidwe kanyengo m’malo mwa ka gulu kochedwa [Accelerating the Impact of CGIAR Climate Research for Africa (AICCRA) Ngakhale kuti pali njira zambiri paulimi okonzekera ndi kubyala mbeu zosiyana- siyana, buku ili colinga cake ndi cogwirizanitsira pa ulimi wansomba. Buku ili lifunika kukhala monga bwenzi” pakachitidwe kamakono kwa alimi ang’ono- ang’ono osunga nsomba za tilapia m’dambo muno m’Zambia. Izi zili tero chifukwa njira zabwino zakayendetsedwe ndikofunkira pakupirira ndi kukhala okonzekera. Kulowerapo pa tinsomba ting’ono, chakudya ndiponso uthenga umene uli pa kulima bwino potsatira nthawi yanyengo ndikofunikira kuthandizira alimi ang’ono-ang’ono pakukolola ndikukhala opirira kukasinthidwe kwanyengo ndipo, potsirizira kuwonjezera chakudya ndipo cakudya cathanzi ndi ndalama.
1.2 Kulinganiza zolinga kwambiri ndi zomwe dziko lifuna

Pansi pagulu lopereka zinthu patsogolo (INDC), dziko la Zambia lifuna kukhala lodzidalira pa chakudya, polima mbeu zosiyanasiyana pokwezeka ulimi wabwino potsatira kwanyengo kuli mbeu, ziweto ndi ulimi wa nsomba, kuwonjezera pa kasungidwe kabwino kumbeu kotero kuti nyama monga nkhumba ndi zinazake zam’thengo ndi zolingana. Chofunikira chimene chiri pa mndandanda ndi kuwauza kupereka ulimi waansomba patsogolo pogwiritsa nchito njira zabwino zamadzi ndi kadyetsedwe ndiponso pogwiritsa nchito nsomba zoyenera. Kugwirizanitsa paulimi wansomba kuthandiza kugwiritsa bwino madzi ndi kuperekanso patsogolo kadyetsedwe ndi kupanga alimi olimbikira, ndiponso kuwonjezera pa zolinga zagulu lofuna kupititsa chitukuko patsogolo m’Zambia. (INDC)

Ngakhale nditero, pa kafukufuku wa kasinthidwe kanyengo momwe tingakhalire olimbikira m’dziko la Zambia anafotokoza kuchita njira zamakono pogwiritsa nchito bwino nthaka, madzi ndi usodzi. (Zambia Intended Nationally Determined Contribution INDC 2015p; xiii). Pansi pa njira izi zamakono, pokonzekera njira popirira pa malimidwe ndi kudzikhalira odala pa chakudya powonjezera njira zophatikizidwa pamodzi ndi alimi a ziweto, nsomba mbalame ndiponso ulimi wandiwo zamasamba [Zambia Intended Nationally Determined Contribution (INDC, p:xiv). Njira izi zamakono kuphatikizapo ulimi zimawonjezera ku Zambia Climate Change Gender Action Plan (IUCN 2017), kuwonjezera kusamala bwino m’dambo mmene azimai ndi anthu enanso osauka amapulumukiramo.
1.3 Chiyembekezo cha zotulukamo
Amene adzapeza phindu afunikira kudziwa izi:
• Kudziwa zinthu zofunikira zakusintha kwanyengo.
• Kudziwa pakasinthidwe ndi njira zodzichepetseramo ngati nyengo yawonekera ndi zobvuta.
• Kudziwa mmene angaziganizire ndi kukhalira olimbikira pakasinthidwe kanyengo pa malimidwe awo.
• Kudziwa pa zinthu zofunikira zokhala okonzekera ndi kulimba panyengo ndi mmene zingagwirire nchito.
• Mopezera uthenga mmene angazichinjirize pakasinthidwe kanyengo powonjezera nzeru popititsa patsogolo luso panthawi ino ya kusintha kwa nyengo.
2.1 Nyengo yapanthawi ndiponso nyengo yokhudza dera kapena malo
Nyengo yokhudza dera amakonda kuyiyerekeza ndi nyengo yapakanthawi, ngakhale ndi tero, nyengo izi ziwiri ndizosiyana.

Nyengo yapanthawi ingasinthe tsiku ndi tsiku kapena chaka ndi chaka. Itanthauza maonekedwe amalo kapena dera. Mwachitsanzo, ngati kuli chimphepo chachikulu kapena kuli mvula kubwalo, iyi ifotokoza m’mene nyengo yatsikulo iliri. Motero, tingakambe kuti nyengo lero kuli mvula kapena chimphepo chachikulu. Nyengo yokhudza malo kapena dera imakamba maonekedwe oyembekezeka kudera panthawi pachaka, iwoneka powona nyengo yapakanthawi pazaka zambiri.
e Malimidwe okonzekera ndi olimba panyengo paulimi wansomba: Kugwirizanitsa ulimi wansomba ndi ulimi waziweto zing’ono-zing’ono
Nyengo yokhudza dera mowonjezerapo kutentha kwa kanthawi ndi kagwedwe kamvula moyerekeza, ndiponso mawombedwe amphepo. Malo osiyana ali ndi nyengo yake.
Izi zotsatira ndizitsanzo zanyengo yokhudzana padera:
• Chipululu ndi malo ouma anyengo yokhudza dera chifukwa malo awa magwedwe amvula achepa kapena madzi oumbana m’chaka.
• Nyengo itentha mopitilira ndiponso kumakhala ko kozizira mopitilira mnthawi yamphepo. • Nyengo kumalo kuli mitengo yambiri kukhala kotentha ndiponso kothumira.
2.1.1 Kodi nyengo muno m’Zambia ili bwanji?

M’Zambia tikambe kuti nyengo ili yotentha kwambiri mwinanso ili pakati potentha, kulingana ndi malo mmene aliri muutali mokhudzana ndi kumlengalenga. Kuchokera pakati pa mwezi waKafwiritsira (November) kufikira m’mwezi wa Kafukulira (March) ndi nyengo ya mvula mdziko, nthawiyi ili yotentha kwambiri komanso pang’ono, ndipo Kuchokera mu mwezi wa Masika (April) kufikira m’mwezi wa Kafwiritsira (November) ndi nyengo youma. Pakati pa mwezi wa Masika (April) kufikira pakati pa mwezi wa Phukira(August) m’Zambia kumakhala kozizira, ndipo pakati pa mwezi wa Changululu (September) ndi pakati pa mwezi wa Kafwiritsira (November), kumatentha komanso kukhala kouma.
2.2 Kodi kusintha kwa nyengo ndi chiyani?

Kusintha kwa nyengo ndi kunena kusintha kwa kuzizira kapena kutentha ndi kusintha kwa nyengo kwa panthawi yaitali kudera. Kusintha kwa nyengo padziko lapansi kumachitika pa pakatikati kwa panthawi yaitali padziko lapansi. Izi mowonjezerapo kutentha ndiponso kagwedwe (kamvula kapena madzi oumbana) ndipo kungachitike kulingana ndi zacilengedwe kapena chifukwa chazochita za anthu. Nyengo yapadziko lapansi yakhala ili kusintha nthawi ndi nthawi, kale kale ngakhale anthu asanalengedwe. Ngakhale ziritero, anthu odziwa zachilengedwe akuwoona zinthu zodabwitsa kwatsopano apa. Mwachitsanzo, kutentha kwa dziko lapansi moyerekeza kwakhala kuli kutentha mosaganizirika kwa zaka dzana limodzi ndi makumi asanu (zaka 150). Kulingana ndi kagulu kochedwa Royal Society, kuyambira m’chaka cha 1900, dziko lapansi kutentha kwake kwakwera ndi moyerekeza ndi 1 digiri seshasi moyerekeza chabe.

Kusintha kwa nyengo kungabweretse kusintha kwa nyengo imene siyidziwika bwino-bwino. Mwachitsanzo, kumalo ena kungabwere mvula yachi mphepo chachikulu yomwe sanaiwonepo, kubweretsa mvula yambiri, madzi yosefukira, chimphepo chachikulu chowononga ndi kupha miyoyo ya anthu.kumalo enanso kumakhalachilala ndi kusefukira kwa madzi.

Ngati nyengo kapena kagwedwe kamvula sikadziwika, chikhala chinthu chobvuta kupanga ndondomeko yaulimi wansomba ndi ulimi wina. Kusadziwika uku kufunikira kudziwa mbiri yazanyengo pofuna kupereka patsogolo zocita zabwino zanyengo zamasiku ano pobweretsa chakudya chambiri chifukwa cha kusintha kwa nyengo.
2.2.1 Kusintha kwa nyengo m’Zambia

M’Zambia, kusinthana pakati pa chilala ndi madzi yosefukira dziko lidzakumana ndi zobvuta zambiri. Kudzaonjezera bvuto lomira, matenda amene abwera chifukwa chakusintha kwanyengo, kubuka kwamatenda ochokera kuzitsamba, kunyama ndiponso ndi ku anthu. Adzaononganso mbeu zolima, miseu, nyumba zambiri, magetsi ndiponso zomangamanga zobweretsa madzi, kusokoneza opereka thandizo la zaumoyo, zakudya kumene kudzapangitsa kuchepekela kwachakudya ndi kuonjezera matenda anjala kapena kusowekera kwachakudya. Kusintha kwa nyengo mwina kudzabweretsa unyinji wa anthu kuchotsedwa m’madera awo m’Zambia, kubweretsa nkhawa, ndi kukhumudwa komanso kuchuluka kwa anthu kukhala malo amodzi.

2.2.2 Kodi chimene chimabweretsa kusintha kwa nyengo ndi chiyani?
2.2.2.1 Zochita za anthu

Izi ndi zinthu zimene amachita anthu zimene zitulutsa utsi woipa ndiponso zimene zichepetsa mphepo yogwira dzuwa mum’lengalenga. Pali zinthu zambiri zimene zibweretsa kusintha kwanyengo. Apa tsopano, tingochulako zochepa chabe. Pogwiritsa nchito mafuta ochokera kuzinthu zopanda moyo monga malasha a miyala, mafuta ndi mpweya zimene zitipatsa mphamvu, zotulutsa utsi woipa, monga mphepo yoipa. Izi zibweretsa utsi woipa mu’mlengalenga kuchepa mphepo yoteteza mum’lengalenga, pothera zibweretsa utsi woipa (kutentha).
Kudula mitengo chiduledule ndi kusasamalira nthaka nakonso kuchepetsa kubvika utsi. Usodzi ndi ulimi wa nsomba suwononga kwambiri mpweya monga zina izi zachulidwa.
2.2.2.2 Njira ya zacilengedwe

Izi ndi zinthu zosiyana siyana zimene zisintha kapangidwe kadziko lapansi kwa nthawi yaitali. Apa tidzayang’anapo njira zitatu; m’mene dzuwa liwalira, m’mene limazungulira Dziko la pansi ndi kuphulika kwa mapiri. Chimene chibweretsa kutentha kwambiri padziko lapansi ndi dzuwa. Motero, kusintha kwa kozungulira pobweretsa kutentha chifukwa chochuluka ndi kabvekedwe kake kungabweretse kusintha pa nyengo ya dera. Ngati ululu wadzuwa ndi wambiri utulutsidwa, ndiye kuti padziko lapansi padzatentha.

Dziko lapansi lili ndi njira zake zachilengedwe mozithumitsira ndi kuziziritsira kupangitsidwa chifukwa cha kusintha kapendekedwe kapena pa kazungulidwe ka dziko kudzuwa. Ngati utali pakati padziko ndi dzuwa kwasiyana panthawi yaitali, kudzakhala kusintha kwa mphamvu ya dzuwa kufika pa dziko la pansi nthawi ndi nthawi kupangitsa kusintha kwa nyengo.

Kuphulika kwa mapiri kubweretsa zotuluka zosakanizika ndizobwera pa nyengo. Kutulutsa zinthu zimene zipangitsa dziko lapansi kuzizira, komanso kutuluka mphepo yoipa, imene ipangitsa kutentha. Ngakhale kuti kuphulika kwa mapir i kupangitsa kusintha kwa nyengo kwa nthawi yaifupi ndi kuonjezera kwa chilengedwe pakusintha kwa nyengo motero, sinjira imene ibweretsa kwambiri kutentha padziko lapansi. Kuzizira ndiko kumene kwenikweni kubweretsa kuphulika kwa mapiri, osati kutentha.
2.3 Kuyankha pa kusintha kwanyengo
2.3.1 Kukonzekera pa kusintha kwanyengo

Kumeneku kutanthauza’’ kusintha mkhalidwe, njira, ndiponso-mnjira ina—njira yaumoyo motetezeramo mabanja, nkhani ya zacuma chathu, kumalo kumene tikhala kuli kusintha kwa nyengo” (WWF, nd). Ngakhale kuchepetsa mphepo yoipa mumlengalenga kunga chepetse zobwera chifukwa chakusintha kwa nyengo mtsogolo ndi kukhala okonzekera bwino, kusintha kwina kwa nyengo kumene kwachitika kale sikungabwezedwe ndichabwino kukhala okonzekera tsopano. Kukhala okonzekera kufunika kusintha njira, zochita, ndipo kapangidwe kochepetsako kuwonongeka kapena kupeza bwino ndi zomwe zotsatira zake chifukwa chakusintha kwa nyengo.’(UNFCCC, nd). Kukonzekera kubweretsa zochita ndikupeza mayankho tsopano ndi kusintha kwa nyengo mtsogolo ndi zotsatirapo. Kusunga mtundu wansomba umene uli olimba kukasinthidwe ka nyengo chingakhale chitsanzo chimodzi chakukonzekera kwakusintha kwa nyengo.
2.3.2 Zinthu zochepetsa pa kusintha kwa nyengo

Chimenechi chitanthauza’’ kupanga zotsatirapo chifukwa cha kusintha kwa nyengo kukhala kopepuka poletsa kapena kuchepetsa kutulutsa mphepo yoipa mu mlengalenga ”(EEA, nd). Ngati tichepetsa kutulutsa mphepo yoipa tsopano apa, chidzakhala chapafupi kukhala okonzekera kusintha kumene sitingapewe.

Ngati tichepetsa kutulutsa utsi woipa, tiletsa kapena kuchepetsa m’mene dziko lapansi litenthera ndiponso kupewetsa kutentha kwambiri kumene kungapangitse kuti umoyo ukhale pa mabvuto pano padziko lapansi. Kukonzekera kungakwaniritsidwe pakuchepetsa mwina kumene kuchokera utsi woipa- mwachitsanzo pochulukitsa kochokera magetsi amene angabwererenso, kapena popanga njira zoyenera zimene ziyenda-kapena poonjezera malo oikamo mpweya woipa — mwachitsanzo, pokulitsa malo a thengo. Mwachidule, kuchepetsa nchito imene munthu achita pofuna kuchepetsako kumene kuchokera mphepo yoipa ndipo kapena kupangitsa kuti mphepo imeneyo isamachoke yambiri.”(EEA, nd)

Mwachitsanzo, kubyala mitengo ndi kuleka kudula mitengo ndi njira imodzi yotetezeramo, chifukwa ipangitsa mitengo kugwira mphepo yoipa m’malo mochotsa mphepo pakuti imalola kugwiridwa ndi mitengo m’malo mwakuti itulutsidwe mu mlengalenga. Njira za kukonzekera paulimi wansomba, mwina, tingawonjezerepo kukhala njira zaubwenzi za tsopano ndizochita komanso kugwiritsa nchito bwino madzi paulimi wansomba, pakuwonjezerapo kukhala ndi malo abwino tsopano komanso kugwiritsa nchito bwino madzi, chimene chingapangitse kagwiritsidwe kamadzi bwino ndi kuchepetsa kuwononga madzi poikamo zinthu zoipa.
2.3.3 Kukonzekera kunyengo

Chimenechi ndiko kuti” kukhala okonzeka, kukwaniritsa kubwerera pakale, ndiponso kukonzeka pa zotsatira chifukwa chakusintha kwa nyengo (C2ES 2019). Pofuna kukhala okonzeka, kufunika kukhala omvetsetsa ndi kudziwa m’mene zinthu zilili zobvuta pofuna kukhala okonzekera,ndi kulimbana nazo. Njira imene ndiyosakonzekera singakwaniritse kuzikonzanso pa zobvuta. Ngati munthu aliyense pa yekha, anthu ali m’ banja ndianthu onse m’dera ndi njira zina sakwanitsa kulongosola pa zotsatira chifukwa chosintha kwa nyengo, ndiponso, m’mene chitukuko chiyendera kungawapangitse kukhala osauka kwambiri, monga mukonera pa chithunzi 1.
Chithunzi choyamba Njira imene singakwaniritse kulimbana ndi zodabwitsa.

2.3.5 Zotsatira pa kusintha kwa nyengo pa ulimi wansomba

Ulimi wansomba uli pamndandanda wa zoipa zimene zimakhudzidwa pa zotsatira zakusintha kwa nyengo, zotsatira ndi matanthauzo akuti pali zoipa ndi zabwino. pai ulimi wansomba, nyengo yotentha pakati pa mtundu wansomba umene ulimbikira upangitsa mtundu wansomba watilapia kusungidwa bwino ndi mitundu ina imene ifuna mazi am’malo ofunda , pamene kusefukira kwa madzi kumalo kotera kungapangits madzi kuchuluka kumadambo amadzi osungirako nsomba. Nthawi yaitali yotentha ingabweretsenso nthawi yaitali yokulirapo ku mitundu ina yansomba, monga tilapia, kuonjezerapo kufunikira kwansomba zosunga chifukwa chosowekera ku nsomba zochita kugwira.

Ngakhale nditero, zoipa zobwera chifukwa chakusintha kwanyengo zipambana zabwino paulimi wansomba. Kudula kwa zinthu zaulimi wa nsomba kumakhudza kwambiri alimi ang’ono- ang’ono pakuti alibe thandizo, monga inshuwarensi (insurance).
Zinthu zotsatirazi ndizimene zimabwera chifukwa chakusintha kwa nyengo paulimi wansomba:
• Kutentha kwa nyengo, kopitirira muyeso, kungabweretse kufa kwambiri ku mitundu ina ya nsomba.

• Kusintha kwa nyengo kubweretsa unyinji watuzilombo mongapalazitiki (parasitic), vairo (viral) ndi matenda a fango (Fungal) [Maulu et al, 2021], mwakuti nsomba zingagwidwe kumatenda awa pamene nyengo itentha. Kutentha kwambiri kungabweretse matenda ochokera kuzomera.

Alimi onse ang’ono ang’ono amapeza mabvuto amene abwera chifukwa cha kusintha kwa nyengo. M’Zambia, azimai adalira m’dambo, kumene kugwiritsidwa nchito po nsomba (IUCN 2017). Ngati madzi abwino akhudzidwa, mabanja ambiri amadwala matenda ochokera kumadzi ndipo sapeza phindu. Pogwiritsa nchito bwino madzi,monga kugwiritsa ulimi wabwino wansomba, umene upititsa patsogolo madzi abwino monga kuchita njira zaulimi wabwino wansombandipo azimai odalira mdambo adzapeza phindu. Ulimi wabwino wansomba ndi kukhala okonzekera ndi olimba potsatira nyengo imene tifuna kugwiritsa nchito bwino madzi ndikukhala okonzekera pakusintha kwa nyengo. Ndi njira yophatikiza imene iwonjezera kusintha ndiponso kuchepetsa m’njira imene ipititsa patsogolo ulimi wansomba pokolola ndi kukhala ndi chakudya ngakhale kuti kuli kusintha kwa nyengo. Ulimi wabwino wansomba ndi kukhala okonzekera ndi olimba potsatira nyengo imene iyankha zobvuta pofuna kukonza zinthu pakati pazolinga pakusintha kwa nyengo pochepetsa, kusintha ndi zokolola, komanso kuonjezera phindu. Pochita usodzi potsata njira zakusintha kwanyengo ndi ulimi wansomba kufunikira njira zabwino pogwiritsa nchitu zinthu zachilengedwe pokolola nsomba ndi chakudya cham’madzi. Chimenechi chipangitsa kukhala olimba m’malo mosungira somba ndi anthu amene adalira pokolola nsomba, kulola mbali imeneyo kuthandiza kupereka chitukuko patsogolo. Ulimi wabwino wansomba pokhala okonzekera ndi olimba potsatira nyengo kufunanso kukhala omvetsetsa njira m’mene tingachepetsere kubvutika kwa amene angakhudzidwe moipa chifukwa chakusintha kwa nyengo (Ahmed and Solomon 2017).

Ulimi wabwino wansomba ndi kukhala okonzekera ndi olimba potsatira nyengo yogwiritsa nchito njira zambiri zaulimi wansomba ndi njira zatsopano. Zimenezi kuphatikizapo ndi kugwirizanitsa paulimi wansomba monga njira yokhazikika pokhala okonzeka pa zobwera chifukwa chakusintha kwanyengo, kupangitsa kugwiritsa nchito zachilengedwe mwaubwino ndi kukolola zambiri pafamu. Blog The private sector is helping to scale the adoption of climate-smart aquaculture in Zambia - boosting women s role one pond at a time published onFebruary 27, 2024 Zambia Aquaculture In Zambia a landlocked country aquaculture provides a critical source of affordable protein. Scaling training programs developed by WorldFish and supported through AICCRA Zambia partnerships are reaching thousands of fish farmers with practices that are boosting productivity by 70 percent and providing women with a more powerful role in production. According to a report led by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), fish is an important source of key micronutrients including vitamin B12, calcium, vitamin D, iodine, and selenium, and of essential fatty acids in the omega-3 family. In Zambia, fish is an affordable source of animal protein. But due to declining stocks of fish caused by overfishing, unsustainable fishing methods, and the impacts of climate change, the gap between the demand for and supply of fish has widened sharply in recent years. Zambia can only supply 85,000 metric tonnes of fish per year, whereas demand exceeds 180,000 metric tonnes annualy. This means that demand is mostly met mostly through imports of fish. For more resilient livelihoods and greater food security in Zambia, it is vital that increased demand for fish is met by increased production through methods such as aquaculture, and that fish production methods are sustainable. Aquaculture refers to the farming of fish and other aquatic animals. Cecilia Zulu is one of a new cohort of women in Zambia now embarking on aquaculture. She proudly shows off her two fishponds, which total 560 square metres. My husband began the aquaculture project, but as time passed, he handed over the operations and management to me, Cecilia explains. Business accelerators for aquaculture SMEs Cecilia received capacity development and training on aquaculture production through an Aquaculture Accelerator led by WorldFish, a CGIAR research center that leads scientific research on aquatic food systems. The WorldFish accelerator has been providing technical support and private sector partners such as EUNIMOS, a Zambian agriculture, aquaculture and food production small-to-medium-sized enterprise (SME), one of several that have been trained to help farmers establish fishponds. The training that Cecilia enjoyed focused particularly on climate-smart elements of aquaculture, which has helped her to be an effective and efficient fish farmer in a fast changing climate in Southern Africa. Climate-smart aquaculture makes use of climatic information to plan aquaculture production. For effective production, aquaculture farmers must understand changes in climate variability, which impacts the timing of cycles of production. With climate-smart aquaculture, farmers can select sites for fishpond construction, design fishponds for flood or drought-prone area, select appropriate fish species to stock, time fish harvests and control water quality in the fishpond. In her training, Cecilia and other fish farmers like her learned about key concepts in relation to the weather, climate change, resilience, mitigation, vulnerability, gender, and the importance of integrating both aquaculture and agriculture systems in her community. The training involved games and decision-making roleplay for critical tasks like site selection, choosing fish species and integrating crops and livestock with aquaculture - depending on rainfall or even floods and droughts. These games helped Cecilia and the other participants understand how theoretical concepts can be applied in real life. Complementary extension information on fish farming, as well as continued mentorship and coaching, is provided through the private sector and government. According to Benson Chongo, Managing Director of EUNIMOS, demonstration aquaculture ponds were critical to effectiveness of the training. They provide hands-on experience for fish farmers to go beyond theoretical training and learn by doing, some of which were conducted at EUNIMOS plots. The project was focused on overcoming the barriers to training that women like Cecilia often face in accessing, using, and controlling aquaculture production. Capture fisheries that is, the catching fish directly from water bodies had largely been seen as a role for men in the communities, whereas women were only involved in processing and marketing. So, the trainings also targeted women and youth specifically, to promote more inclusivity in aquaculture production. Other ways women fish farmers were reached with training include farmer roadshows and targeted radio programs, which has seen an increase in the participation of Zambian women in aquaculture. Thanks to the Accelerating Impacts of CGIAR Climate Research in Africa (AICCRA) project, which is backed by the World Bank Group, such training is now being delivered on a larger scale in Zambia. AICCRA partnerships across Africa are led by many CGIAR centers and over 90 partner organisations. In Zambia, AICCRA's work is led by the International Water Management Institute (IMWI). Under the initial aquaculture accelerator, WorldFish worked with four SMEs in northern Zambia, reaching 2,341 farmers in 2020. 14 percent of them were women. But with AICCRA scaling support, the accelerator expanded to six SMEs, with AICCRA providing a grant of USD 50,000. In 2022, the number of beneficiaries increased to 15,781 and nearly half of the attendees were women in that year. Maintaining momentum over three years, in total some 45,154 farmers have been reached by these collaborative efforts, with 36 percent of the total reached being women. Cecilia s story Cecilia has eagerly adopted what she learned in the training. She now uses droppings from her chickens and manure from her pigs as additional feed for her fish. She also uses the nutrient rich wastewater from the ponds to irrigate vegetables that also provide additional feed for the fish. Cecilia proudly notes that now she can decide whether to harvest fish for her own family s consumption or whether to sell it at market - without seeking her husband's permission. Before I started getting into aquaculture things were hard now I can personally make decisions to get fish to feed my family or to sell. my neighbors admire what I do, and they also want to have fishponds."" She pointed out that this potential additional income from aquaculture has led to improved nutritional and educational outcomes for her children, as she can now more easily afford school equipment or medical prescriptions when they are needed. Cecilia is encouraging women to invest in aquaculture, one pond at a time , as it will increase the well-being of their households. Another farmer, Lydia, reflected on how her agency within the community have increased, noting that: As long as you are willing to work hard and not scared of the mud, you will significantly improve your livelihood . AICCRA's approach demonstrated the importance of the private sector partners as a viable scaling pathway particularly leveraging the potential of agribusiness SMEs. It starts with the identification of viable private sector firms willing to invest in smallholder aquaculture. It then demands reliable input and output markets in climate-smart aquaculture technologies, for win-win situations that benefit both the private sector and smallholder farmers. Farmers win with the availability of a reliable markets for fish and quality fingerlings. Meanwhile the private gains farmers who want to buy inputs from their businesses. Critically, AICCRA s grants de-risked the cost of investment in smallholder aquaculture for the six SMEs in its accelerator program. Alongside EUNIMOS was Triple Blessings Center, Kasakalabwe Multi-purpose Cooperative Society, ADSEK Enterprises Ltd, Kasama Arts Theatre, and Hope Ways Enterprises. As the AICCRA project looks to continue scaling innovation, thanks to additional finance from the World Bank, this private sector-led scaling pathway will be expanded in other provinces within Zambia to ensure that aquaculture farmers have access to and are using climate information services to transform livelihoods for all. Short impact statement

The aquaculture practices among smallholder fish farmers in Northern Zambia are undergoing a remarkable transformation driven by climate smart aquaculture solutions implemented by the AICCRA project in the region. For a long time, fish farmers have faced challenges of low temperatures, erratic rainfall pattern affecting water quality in the fishponds, limited access to fingerlings and knowledge on land-based aquaculture best management practices in the face of climate change.

Today, thanks to the AICCRA project, smallholder fish farmers are embracing innovative approaches to aquaculture. The project has not only improved their farming techniques but also significantly enhanced their livelihoods by empowering them with climate-smart aquaculture technologies; strengthening their resilience through access to important weather information; and linked them to aquaculture markets to sustainably improve income and food security and quality of life. The project is transforming the way fish farming is practiced in the region, creating more resilient communities and sustainable farming systems.
Introduction

AICCRA Zambia is scaling access to and use of climate-smart services and innovations to help Zambian farmers and communities safeguard their livelihoods in the face of climate change. AICCRA is Accelerating Impacts of CGIAR Climate Research for Africa. Climate change is threatening Zambia’s aquaculture and livestock systems, impacting agriculture businesses and undermining livelihoods. It is increasingly urgent for fish farmers in Zambia to be able to anticipate climate-related events and take appropriate preventative actions. AICCRA Zambia is working with

local and national partners to scale actionable climate information, de-risk investments into agribusinesses and boost the knowledge and use of climate-smart aquaculture technologies which promote gender and social inclusion.
Intervention description

Since 2021, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), in partnership with WorldFish and other local organizations, has collaborated with SMEs in the aquaculture value chain to scale actionable climate-smart agriculture (CSA) and climate information services (CIS) innovation bundles. These efforts aim to enhance smallholder farmers’ water and food security while building resilience to climate shocks.

The project partners with the private sector to co-design and implement accelerator grants for startups/SMEs, reducing the risks associated with scaling innovations. This approach enhances the climate resilience of value chains, promotes social inclusion, and ensures the sustainable use of land and water resources. Under the aquaculture innovation bundle, six SMEs in the aquaculture sector received accelerator grants to scale the adoption of climate-smart aquaculture among smallholder fish farmers. These SMEs are: EUNIMOS Investment, Kasakalabwe Multipurpose Cooperative Society, Kasama Arts Theatre, Triple Blessings Centre, HopeWays, and ADSEK Enterprise Limited (https://hdl.handle.net/10568/117963).

Each SME offers unique services within the aquaculture value chain, operating under a business model that integrates CSA and CIS extension services. The ultimate goal is to empower farmers to adopt climate-smart technologies, increasing their resilience and productivity while creating demand for SME products, including seeds, feed, and agro-veterinary supplies.
To facilitate the adoption of climate-smart technologies, the project implemented several interventions:

• Technical Support and Capacity Building WorldFish provided technical support to SMEs, enhancing their capacity to deliver high-quality CSA and CIS extension services. See https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12348/5596. Training sessions focused on integrated fish- livestock systems and Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI). These ensured that CSA approaches and CIS access addressed and reduced gender and social disparities, empowering women, girls, and disadvantaged groups. https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12348/5596. See

• Multistakeholder Platforms. A multistakeholder platform was established to promote integrated aquaculture-agriculture systems. This platform facilitated information sharing and strengthened linkages between private sector actors and smallholder farmers (https://hdl.handle.net/10568/127029).

• Radio Programs and Roadshows. The SMEs conducted joint live radio programs on local stations such as Yangeni and Mano. These programs disseminated CSA and CIS information to smallholder farmers. Additionally, roadshows showcased everyday
challenges farmers face, such as floods, droughts, and pests, while providing practical solutions and contact information for SMEs.

• Digital Information Sharing. The partnership created a WhatsApp group to enhance information dissemination. Managed by SMEs, the group includes members from the Zambia Meteorological Department (ZMD), Extension officers from the department of fisheries, WorldFish, and lead farmers. Daily weather bulletins from ZMD are shared directly with farmers, helping them plan their farming activities effectively.
Results of the intervention

In Northern Zambia, the livelihoods of smallholder fish farmers are being transformed through innovative climate-smart aquaculture solutions introduced in partnership with SMEs engaged by the AICCRA project. Six SMEs were enlisted to scale the adoption of these technologies in the region: EUNIMOS Investment, HopeWays, Kasakalabwe Multipurpose Cooperative Society, Kasama Arts Theatre, Triple Blessings Centre, and ADSEK Enterprise Limited.

Over 15,700 farmers have adopted sustainable farming practices, gained access to millions of fingerlings, and secured fish output markets offering premium prices for farmed fish. The project has introduced practical solutions to mitigate the impacts of climate change, such as integrated farming systems. Farmers now combine aquaculture with livestock and crop farming, utilizing livestock droppings as pond fertilizers to enhance phytoplankton growth, which improves fish nutrition and increases oxygen levels in the ponds.

Furthermore, farmers have adopted the design of modern fishponds capable of withstanding flooding and drought, significantly reducing fish losses during climate shocks. Before this initiative, farmers frequently lost fish during flash floods as they escaped from poorly designed ponds. Similarly, erratic rainfall caused water levels to drop, leading to fishponds drying out and forcing farmers to harvest fish prematurely, often before they reached market size. Focus Group Discussions with the beneficiaries revealed that farmers now receive timely weather information updates from the Zambia Metrological Department (ZMD) via WhatsApp and radio, helping them plan farming activities more effectively.
The farmers shared experiences, explaining how the training he received transformed the fish farming practices:

“It has helped me reduce fish losses and improve water management and water quality in the fishponds. I use the information to prepare my fishponds, so they don’t get flooded, preventing fish from escaping. My ponds are designed with an inlet that allows water to enter and an outlet to drain excess water. When there’s too much rainfall, I use the outlet to prevent overflow.”

“In cases of inadequate rainfall, when water levels go down, I dig deeper into the water source to channel more water into the ponds using the drainage system connected to each inlet. This process requires climate information on early warning systems to help me prepare when to drain the fishpond and when to increase water flow from the underground source using the drainage.” Paul explains the process for managing water quality and water levels in his fishponds.

“Before this initiative, we didn’t pay attention to weather forecasts, now, farmers rely on this information to make decisions, reducing climate risks.” Collins explains improvements made in using climate information.

Furthermore, discussions with the farmers revealed that the AICCCRA project has brought tangible improvements to the lives of smallholder farmers. The farmers have stressed that they have seen notable changes in their aquaculture operations and incomes. While precise income figures are difficult to capture due to partial harvest practices, farmers report significant improvements in their livelihoods.

“Our knowledge has advanced; we know about fishpond modern fishpond construction, temperature monitoring, water quality, feeding practices, and biosecurity. This has helped us improve our farming practices to optimise production amid climate shocks, ensuring food security and a steady income.” Florence explains how access to enhanced knowledge on aquaculture has helped to improve farming practices and yield.
“Previously, our management was very poor,” said Nathan. “We used to lose a lot of fish, but now we have seen improvements. The fish grow, and we don’t lose as many.”

Farmers acknowledged the broader socioeconomic benefits of their improved practices. With better yields, households can address urgent household needs, from school uniforms for their children to medical expenses, enhancing their overall quality of life.

Ukulondolola pa ifitekwa na ifilimwa ifya mu menshi kutila bulimi ubwa ifi ifintu. Zambia eyaba nangu iya ukulenga mutanda (6) mu fyalo ifikalamba ifya iposa mu ubulimi ubwa isabi mu Africa. Ukwela nangu ukwikata isabi cila mwaka ukufuma mu ifishiba kwalininine pa mulu apakalamba ukufuma ku cipendo ica ubufino ubwa amatani 5,000 (Ton) mu 2005 ukufika mupepi na amatani 30,000 (Ton) mu 2016.
