Hoy, crear cadenas más equitativas se ha convertido en una prioridad. En algunos casos, para lograr esto las empresas están uniéndose a Sistemas de Sostenibilidad Voluntarios (VSS por sus siglas en inglés), estos son: ""mecanismos basados en el mercado, desarrollados por actores privados… y diseñados para abordar retos sociales y medioambientales mediante la definición de prácticas responsables y la medición del rendimiento de los actores en las cadenas de valor” (Morgan and Zaremba, 2023, p.7).

Inicialmente las guías y estándares sociales y medio ambientales a los que las empresas se adherían eran establecidos por terceros, mayoritariamente ONGs. Hoy varias empresas, con la asesoría de ONGs, han desarrollado sus propios sistemas de sostenibilidad conocidos como “company-led” o “Industry-led standards”. En el caso del café, Starbucks C.A.F.E. Practices y Nespresso AAA son los más conocidos (Grabs, 2018).

Aunque tradicionalmente estos estándares se enfocan en atributos ambientales o comercio justo, cada vez más incorporan elementos relacionado con equidad de género. Como ejemplo está el Add-on de género de 4C que ofrece a las entidades certificadas por 4C agregar una certificación adicional de género (ver 4C Certification Gender Equality). El Coffee Quality Institute (CQI) en colaboración con The Global Coffee Platform (GCP) construyeron a través de la alianza para la equidad de género (The Partnership for Gender Equity-PGE) el índice de equidad de género para el sector café que empresas como ECOM ha ulitzado para establecer una ruta y plan de acción en sus esfuerzos por mejorar la equidad de género en sus prácticas (Wong, 2021).

Una vez se comprometen, las empresas enfrentan el desafío de traducir sus compromisos en acciones concretas que generan cambios en la equidad de género en su cadena. Un reto es conocer mejor quiénes son los diversos actores, mujeres y grupos marginados, que se involucran en su cadena de suministro. Actualmente, la falta de datos—y específicamente de datos que nos permitan conocer los diferentes tipos de mujeres que participan en la cadena—dificulta:
a) Comprender los diversos roles que diferentes tipos de mujeres tienen en las cadenas y las barreras que impiden mejorar sus medios de subsistencia.
b) Definir acciones dirigidas a incrementar los beneficios que ellas podrían obtener de la cadena (incluidos el empoderamiento económico).
c) Iniciar un aprendizaje adaptativo dentro de las empresas para lograr cadenas de suministro sostenibles en diferentes contextos socioculturales y cadenas productivas (o de negocios).

Para responder a este reto, el presente estudio construyó una tipología de las mujeres que participan en la cadena en base a su rol dentro de ésta, su relación con la empresa y su posición sociocultural. Este análisis permitió identificar grupos diferentes de mujeres para orientar acciones diferenciadas en una misma cadena de valor.

2. Mujeres en la cadena del café: El
caso de Honduras
2.1. Mujeres en la cadena de café a nivel global

Según la Organización Internacional del Café (ICO por sus siglas en inglés) a nivel mundial entre el 20 y 30% de las fincas de café son manejadas por mujeres. Ese mismo estudio indica que ellas aportan cerca del 70% de la mano de obra en la producción de café (dependiendo de la región) (2018). A pesar del importante rol que juegan las mujeres en el café, al igual que otras mujeres en el sector agrícola ellas enfrentan grandes desafíos: a) mayores cargas laborales; b) menores ingresos y menor poder de decisión sobre ellos y sobre la administración de las parcelas; c) menor acceso a tierra y otros activos; d) limitado acceso a crédito debido a la ausencia de activos para acceder a préstamos y e) menor acceso a asistencia técnica y formación (ICO, 2018; SCA, 2018). Todo esto impacta los rendimientos de sus fincas, los ingresos que perciben de su labor, y el bienestar de sus familias y comunidades dado que las mujeres invierten gran parte de esos ingresos en la salud, educación, nutrición y seguridad alimentaria de sus familias (Müller and Casabonne, 2020).
2.2. Mujeres en la cadena de café en Honduras

En Honduras, uno de los países productores de café más importantes a nivel mundial1, la participación de las mujeres en la caficultura no es diferente a la encontrada en otras regiones del mundo donde se observa una proporcion pequeña de mujeres propietarias que contrasta con su significativa participación en la producción del rubro, particularmente en fincas pequeñas (ICO, 2018; SCA, 2018). En Honduras, se estima que 20% de los productores registrados son mujeres (un total de 24, 858 productoras), siendo El Paraíso el municipio con el mayor número de productoras registradas como tal (3,541) (Gobierno, 2020)2. A nivel nacional, como el resto de los productores de café en Honduras, la mayoría de ellas son pequeñas y medianas productoras (94%) (Mogrovejo et al, 2020)3.

Estas cifras representan sólo a las mujeres que cuentan con tierra titulada y registro en IHCAFE. Muchas mujeres productoras no están registradas en IHCAFE ya que, a pesar de tener tierra, los altos costos del proceso de legalización hacen que la mayoría carezca de título de propiedad. Este es un requisito relativamente reciente para poder registrarse como cafetaleras. Por otro lado, la gran mayoría de mujeres que participan en la cadena no tienen tierra. Por lo tanto, los datos convencionales utilizados para cuantificar la participación de las mujeres en la cadena del café muestran sólo una pequeña parte de ellas.

La mayoría de las mujeres involucradas en la cadena del café son miembros de familias productoras. Ellas realizan labores productivas, de procesamiento, cuido de trabajadores y cosecha sin recibir un pago formal por su labor y, en su mayoría, sin ser reconocidas como parte de la cadena. Aquellas empleadas en la cadena, están sobrerrepresentadas en los eslabones menos rentables, generando menos ingresos si llegan a recibirlos (Lara, 2009, Mogrovejo et al, 2020; Accerenzi and Duke, 2023; FAO, 2023). Por ejemplo, Ceballos-Sierra estima que el 50% de quienes están involucrados en la cosecha de café, un empleo temporal y con bajo salario, son mujeres (2022). Ellas participan en otros eslabones considerados mejor remunerados, aunque en menor proporción. En el 2018, solo 12% de los intermediarios registrados en AHICAFE fueron mujeres (Álvarez, 2018)4. Álvarez también señala que las mujeres representan apenas el 23% de los empleados contratados por compañías exportadoras en el sector (2018). Si bien el procesamiento y tostado del café es manejado por compañías grandes, existen algunas pequeñas tostadoras artesanales manejadas por mujeres (AMUCAFEH, 2019) y algunas mujeres exportan directamente su café, en su mayoría a través de cooperativas (Swisscontact, 2021).

En los últimos años, el alto número de hombres productores que han migrado lleva a que más mujeres manejen las fincas familiares, aunque formalmente éstas continúen registras a nombre de sus esposos/padres/hermanos. Ríos et al indican que en Guatemala, Honduras y El Salvador, un tercio de las fincas censadas para su estudio eran lideradas por mujeres (2022), planteando preguntas sobre las barreras específicas que ellas enfrentan dado su nuevo rol y el tipo de asistencia técnica que requieren.

2.3. Los desafíos de las mujeres hondureñas en la cadena del café
Las mujeres hondureñas que participan en la cadena del café enfrentan desafíos simulares a los que viven otras mujeres en la misma cadena a nivel mundial:
1. Menor acceso a la tierra y otros activos y menor acceso a crédito y asistencia financiera (Gobierno de Honduras, 2020; Lara, 2009; Ruben et al., 2018).
2. Menor poder de decisión sobre los ingresos generados por el café, la administración de las fincas y las decisiones sobre el crédito (Dietz et al, 2018; Rubio-Jovel, 2021).
3. Mayor carga laboral dado que las normas dominantes de género les atribuyen todas las responsabilidades domésticas y de cuido, a las que se suman las actividades agrícolas (Rubio-Jovel, 2021).
4. Limitada movilidad que afecta su participación en grupos de mujeres, programas educativos y formación técnica brindada por cooperativas u otras organizaciones (Rubio-Jovel, 2021; Lara, 2009).
5. Menor asistencia técnica porque no son percibidas como productoras y/o asistencia que ignora sus necesidades específicas (Pérez Hernández, et al 2018; Gobierno, 2020; Cui, 2022).

En Honduras también se observan diferencias entre mujeres que participan en la cadena. Rubio-Jovel observó una correlación entre el tamaño de las propiedades de mujeres y su empoderamiento económico: aquellas con más tierra estaban más empoderadas económicamente (2021). Además, contrario a la gran mayoría de mujeres, ellas tienen mayor acceso a crédito, servicios técnicos y capacitación (Accerenzi y Duke, 2023; Pérez Hernández, 2018). La edad y la etnicidad también inciden en la experiencia de las mujeres en la cadena. En la zona Lenca de Honduras, el ingreso de las mujeres Lenca que participan en la cadena del café es casi la mitad del obtenido por hombres Lencas y el de las mujeres jóvenes lencas es aún menor al de las mujeres adultas lencas (cerca de 20% menos) (Pérez Hernández et al, 2018).

Si bien en la última década la participación de las mujeres en la cadena ha sido más visible—hay más mujeres participando en cooperativas y organizaciones cafetaleras (Mogrovejo et al, 2020)—los retos que ellas siguen enfrentando llevaron al gobierno de Honduras a aprobar en el 2021 la Política de Género del Subsector Café, convirtiéndose en el primer país en el mundo en aprobar una política semejante (Rikolto, 2021)5. Esta es considerada un paso esencial para lograr la sostenibilidad social del café, en riesgo—entre varios motivos—por la desigualdad de género y el bajo involucramiento de nuevas generaciones. La premisa básica de la política es que fortalecer la participación de las mujeres en la institucionalidad cafetalera así como su acceso a servicios y recursos contribuirá a lograr mayor producción, mejores ingresos y mayor liderazgo, lo que a su vez conllevará a su inclusión en la cadena. Como la misma política indica, lograr este cometido requerirá la alianza de diversos actores.

Las condiciones de las mujeres en la cadena del café y la diversidad entre ellas es un tema relevante para empresas y otros actores del sector, sin embargo surgen dudas: ¿cómo incluir en el análisis de cadenas, los factores socioculturales que inciden en las diferentes y, en muchos casos, desiguales formas en que las mujeres participan en la cadena? ¿Cuáles factores priorizar en el diseño de acciones? ¿Cómo adaptar las propuestas de solución según los factores priorizados? El estudio que aquí describimos propone una metodología de trabajo que responde a esas preguntas. El fin es apoyar a orientar mejor acciones diferenciadas que empresas y otros actores emprenden para construir cadenas inclusivas, equitativas y sostenibles.

3. Descripción de la metodología

El objetivo del estudio fue identificar quiénes son las mujeres que participan en la cadena de Volcafe en el departamento de El Paraíso y analizar si entre ellas hay mujeres que debido a su posicionalidad social tienen limitaciones y beneficios distintos a otras, con el fin de orientar las inversiones en equidad de género que la empresa hace en esa zona. Identificamos y caracterizamos los diferentes grupos de mujeres a través de la construcción de una tipología de las mujeres que participan en la cadena de la empresa utilizando un enfoque interseccional.
El estudio buscó responder 3 preguntas específicas:
1. ¿Quiénes son las diferentes mujeres que participan en la cadena de la empresa?
2. ¿Qué prácticas en la cadena de la empresa generan beneficios y qué practicas limitan los beneficios que diferentes mujeres obtienen de la cadena?
3. ¿Cómo pueden las empresas crear condiciones propicias que potencien los beneficios para los distintos grupos de mujeres en su cadena de suministro?
3.1. Tipologías en investigación agrícola para el desarrollo y el enfoque interseccional

Las tipologías son una herramienta analítica común para organizar información. Construir tipologías de sujetos consiste en agruparlos en distintos tipos en función de características comunes y diferencias que permitan identificar patrones en sus experiencias (Stapley et al, 2022). Para crear los grupos se utilizan dimensiones relevantes, las cuales derivan de los modelos conceptuales usados y los objetivos de la investigación. Desde el punto de vista analítico, las tipologías pueden facilitar las comparaciones teóricas y, desde el punto de vista empírico, pueden ayudar a desarrollar intervenciones adaptadas. Sin embargo, es siempre importante tomar en cuenta que éstas son abstracciones dinámicas, es decir, son generalizaciones que no son fijas en el tiempo ni en el espacio.

El uso de tipologías en la investigación agrícola no es nuevo. Por ejemplo, se han utilizado tipologías de agricultores para sugerir una mejor adaptación de servicios de extensión o para definir programa de adaptación climática (por ejemplo, Singh, et. al, 2022; Musafiri, et. al, 2020; Shukla, et. al, 2019); sin embargo, estas tipologías han priorizado las características biofísicas de las fincas o las características generales del hogar para realizar las agrupaciones, ignorando en muchos casos las características socioculturales de los actores y cómo estás inciden en las desigualdades rurales (Nguyen-Perperidis, 2023).
Algunos estudios que analizan la participación de las mujeres en las cadenas de valor también se han usado tipologías cualitativas para:
- Comprender la heterogeneidad de las mujeres (Oduol, et al, 2017);
Poner en primer plano la mirada que ellas tienen sobre sus propias vidas (Farnworth et al., 2021);
Identificar patrones en la información obtenida que facilitan diseñar intervenciones adaptadas a las particularidades de los diferentes grupos de mujeres (Oduol, et al, 2017; Friedman et al., 2018 ).

Estos estudios, por lo general se enfocan en mujeres productoras y usan dimensiones como la jefatura del hogar y/o tenencia de la tierra para crear las tipologías, dejando de lado a las mujeres que trabajan en agricultura pero no son vistas como productoras, mujeres en otros eslabones de la cadena, así como los factores socioculturales que inciden en la experiencia de las mujeres. El enfoque interseccional explora cómo la raza, etnicidad, edad, lugar de origen, clase, (entre otros) interactúan con el género y ubican a las mujeres en diferentes posiciones sociales. Estos factores sociocultural y el rol de las mujeres en la cadena inciden en los beneficios que obtienen y los retos que enfrentan.
3.2. Características de la metodología utilizada
La metodología es:
- Cualitativa, utilizando un enfoque etnográfico que provee información contextual y permite ahondar en la diversidad de experiencias que viven las mujeres.
- Participativa, involucrando a la empresa y las mujeres que participan del estudio en la construcción de las tipologías durante todo el proceso.

- Sitio-Específica, comprendiendo las dinámicas locales de la cadena de una empresa para informar acciones relevantes en un sitio específico dirigidas a los diferentes grupos de mujeres. Es decir, los resultados de este estudio no representa todo el universo de mujeres en la región si no las experiencias de aquellas vinculadas a una empresa específica (Volcafe). Tampoco representa a la cadena de café de Volcafe en Honduras ya que tanto la dinámica de su cadena como las mujeres en ella varían entre zonas.

El paso 1 Conceptualización teórica

El objetivo fue comprender el contexto geográfico y sociocultural de la zona y la cadena específica a analizar. Para lograrlo, revisamos la literatura académica y gris sobre la cadena de café a nivel nacional y en la zona de interés. También conversamos con los socios de la investigación: los puntos focales del equipo nacional de la organización internacional Swisscontact y de la empresa Volcafe (Molinos de Honduras) para comprender la cadena en la zona y dialogar sobre el protocolo de investigación. Este paso nos permitió tener un primer mapeo de la cadena en la zona para priorizar sitios a visitar para conocer la diversidad de mujeres participando en ello. La revisión de literatura y el dialogo con socios permitió la identificación de factores socioculturales que inciden en las experiencias de las y los participantes en la cadena y que podrían ser relevantes en la construcción de las tipologías. En base a la conceptualización teórica de la cadena y a las conversaciones con el equipo técnico nacional se construyó un esbozo del mapa de la cadena en El Paraíso que utilizamos como punto de partida en los grupos focales desarrollados en el paso 2. El proceso fue realizado entre finales de septiembre e inicios de octubre del 2023.
Paso 2: Identificación de dimensiones de interés

El objetivo fue comprender la cadena en la zona y las mujeres que a nivel comunitario participan en ella con el fin de identificar dimensiones relevantes que nos permitieran elaborar una primera tipología de mujeres en la cadena de Volcafe en El Paraíso. Utilizamos dos herramientas. La primera fue el mapeo participativo de la cadena en grupos focales y la segunda fueron entrevistas semiestructuradas con informantes claves, principalmente mujeres, en la zona. En esta etapa el equipo de investigación fue conformado por dos antropólogas y fue realizado entre el 16 y el 22 de octubre del 2023.

Definición de grupos focales: El primer grupo focal se realizó con los técnicos de Volcafe en El Paraíso (15 hombres y 1 mujer). Fue importante iniciar con ellos para socializar los objetivos de la investigación, comprender en mayor detalle cómo opera la cadena de la empresa en el departamento, tener una primera descripción de las diferentes mujeres que participan en ella y las variaciones que existen según la zona (en cuanto a la cadena y la participación de mujeres). A partir de ese dialogo, definimos conjuntamente los criterios para seleccionar las zonas donde desarrollamos los demás grupos focales (ver tabla 1).

1. Background

Agriculture and the processing of and trade in food products are notoriously riddled with inequality. Rural women, as well as marginalized groups at the base of agrifood supply chains, typically experience poor terms of trade and are embedded in highly unequal relationships with other actors along the chain. As socio-economic and environmental conditions of global production and trade are increasingly scrutinized, reputational concerns and commitments to corporate social responsibility among medium- to large-scale agrifood companies are motivating companies to reevaluate their practices and provisioning models.

As a result, agrifood companies are increasingly striving to address gender inequalities in value chains to mitigate risks and increase the long-term sustainability of their supply chains. In some cases, companies are voluntarily joining Voluntary Sustainability Systems (VSS), or: “market- based mechanisms developed by private parties (such as NGOs) designed to address social and environmental challenges by defining responsible practices and measuring performance of actors in value chains” (Morgan and Zaremba, 2023). Within VSS, companies adhere to the guidance and standards set by third-party actors to certify their compliance with improved social and environmental standards.

Yet, firms face many challenges in this work. One of these is having a clear line of sight on the diverse actors, including women and marginalized groups, who supply their products. The result is an inadequate understanding of women’s roles in their value chains and of the deep-seated barriers to improving their livelihoods. The lack of data and evidence in this area hampers the design of targeted interventions to enhance and improve women’s participation; the full potential of value chain benefits for women; their economic empowerment through value chains; and gender equality and social inclusion along the supply chain. Likewise, a lack of data – and specifically of data that sheds light on intersectional differences among women – conceals the contributions of diverse groups of women to the value chain, hinders adaptive learning to achieve sustainable supply chains, and limits the capacities of companies to understand, report on and communicate the impacts of their practices on different groups of women, gender equality and social inclusion.
2. Aim and objectives
As such, this toolkit aims to improve gender equality and women’s livelihoods through agrifood value chain development and programming but proposing a methodology to firms and VSS to:

1. Identify the different groups of actors involved in the upstream (producer, processor, trader) nodes of agrifood value chains - with emphasis on hidden or marginalized groups - and the specific roles, contributions, and benefits of these groups in/from the value chain;
2. Identify the specific barriers these differentiated actors experience in the value chain;
3. Find entry points to create a more enabling environment for these groups and/or for tailored programming to support them.
The tools included in this toolkit address the following questions:

1. How does the value chain work, and who are the small-scale value chain actors who manage and/or provide the knowledge, skills and labor to produce, process, and trade in the selected commodities (roles and contributions)?

2. Where in the value chain are different groups of women (by gender, marital status, age, ethnicity, residence status, socio-economic status, etc.) involved, and how do they each contribute to the chain?
3. What benefits (tangible and intangible) and costs/opportunity costs do different groups of women derive or experience in the value chain?
4. How can firms create enabling conditions to enhance those benefits for different groups of women, and particularly marginalized value chain actors?
This document represents a preliminary version of the toolkit that will continue to be developed and piloted in the years to come.
3. Overview of the methodology

The toolkit presents a general methodology for understanding the roles, contributions and challenges of diverse groups of women in agrifood value chains. The process consists of five steps summarized in Table 1.
Step 1: Understanding context and the sector.
The purpose is to gain an understanding of the area and the value chain (e.g., geographical area of importance for the company or VSS or specific node of the value chain) where the

methodology will be implemented. This analysis covers information about operations in that area, statistics disaggregated by gender and other social variables, if available, and background information about firm activities and their gender dimensions. This is achieved via: 1) literature review on the value chain and geography of interest through a gender and social inclusion lens; 2) formative engagement with staff from the buying firm through informal interviews. This step also consists of adapting the research protocol with relevant staff from the firm or VSS and defining the group of actors to include in step 2.
Step 2: Mapping the value chain.

The purpose is to understand the operations of the value chain in the area and identify where and how women and other marginalized groups are involved. Who are the actors in the upstream nodes of the value chain? How do they each contribute to the chain? This is achieved via: 1) focus group discussions (FGD) and 2) semi-structured interviews with key actors in the chain (Tool 1).
Step 3: Creating and validating typologies

The purpose is to create an initial typology of upstream value chain actors and validate it. Based on findings in step 2, identify sociocultural factors (e.g. age, ethnicity, marital status, place of origin, religion, gender) that facilitate or limit the participation, contributions, and benefits of women or marginalized groups in/from the value chain. They will help you create the initial typology. The FGDs provide feedback on the relevance of the initial typologies created and if they need to be changed. 1. Introduction

Crop cut surveys are field surveys in which production data are collected through direct measurement. Crop cutting is the most widely used method of yield estimation throughout the world. The major objective of a crop cut survey is to measure actual crop yields under actual management conditions. In a crop cut survey, yield of a crop is measured from randomly selected sample plots within a crop field. Usually, a sub-plot of a given size is selected at random from each selected plot. The selected sub-plot is harvested by the enumerator and weighed after processing appropriately. Then, the harvested yield per unit area is calculated as the weight of the harvested crop divided by the area of the sub-plot.
2. Section I: Sampling
1. List districts within states based on production intensity of the crop to be surveyed.
2. Within districts, select sub-districts (up to 10) that produce the crop widely.
3. Get a list of households living in the sub-district from local administration or office of agriculture.
4. From the list, prepare a list of those who grow the crop (growers’ list)
5. From the growers list, prepare a list of men and women headed households (head of household list)

6. From the head of housed list, select 15 -20 households depending on area coverage of the crop per local administration unit (proportional to the men and women headed households, see #6 below) that grow the crop depending on head of household list.
7. The men (M) and Women (W) headed households’ proportion can be calculated as: M = M/(M+W) and W = (W/M+W).
3. Section II: Field area measurement

GPS coordinates and area measurement are usually embedded in the ODK, CAPI or KOBO tools as part of a given survey. If the survey uses one of the above-mentioned tools, please record the centroid (central) latitude and longitude of the big plot and measure the area using the polygon option by walking around the perimeter of the plot.
If you are not suing any of the tools, you can use one of the following to record GPS coordinates and measure field or plot area.
i. GPS-based field area measurement

A GPS uses satellite data to determine a geographic position on the earth’s surface based on longitude and latitude. The position is found by a continuous measurement of the time a satellite signal takes to reach your GPS from a satellite in the sky. The GPS can calculate the geographical position with sufficient accuracy (through triangulation) when there are clear signals from at least four satellites. The better sight to a large part of the sky a GPS has, the more signals and clearer signals are received. When using GPS in the field, stay away from the shadows of buildings and even large trees.
Required equipment/materials.

If GPS is not available, use a mobile App. For android phones or tablets, please download “My GPS Location: Realtime” app from google play. (Please note this App may not be accessible in some countries).

Procedure
Step 1: Identify the boundaries of the field to be surveyed.

Step 2: Mark your starting point with a ranging pole, so that you can identify the point when you return. The starting point is suggested to be the northwest corner of the field, to maintain directional consistency.
Step 3: Turn on the GPS device by holding the power button until an image appears on screen. The GPS will then seek to acquire satellite signals. Wait until at least eight signals appear.
Step 4: Go to the main menu.
Step 5: Select “area calculation” and press “start”.

Step 6: Walk slowly clockwise around the perimeter of the field. You should hold the GPS flat in your hand and stretch your hand slightly forward. Walk on the edge of the field (not a meter outside or inside the plot). At every corner, stop for 5 seconds (counting slowly 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5) and then continue walking. You must walk all the way around the field until you return to the corner where you have started.

Step 7: When you reach the starting point, click on “calculate”. The GPS will display the area in square meters. You should then save the results with two decimals. You can change the unit depending on your needs.

Step 8: Save the results by selecting “save”. Delete the default track name and replace it with your specific field ID. The IDs are mostly provided in the form of barcodes or QR codes. Then, press “done”.
Step 9: To review the track, return to the main menu, and navigate to “track manager”. Use “thumb stick” to select the track you would like to review.
Step 10: When you finish, turn off the GPS device by holding the power button. This helps to save power until you identify the next field.

Step 1: Delineate the corners of the sub-plots using stake on all corners.

Step 3: Yield measurement
Step 3.1: Through a 4 m x 4m quadrat and count all the plant population within the quadrant.
Step 3.2: Cut all grain heads (large grains) and above ground part (small grains and legumes) and below ground (ground nut) within the quadrant.
Step 3.3: Remove the grains from the head (this can be done by gentle beating, but may need further drying), weigh and take the moisture content of a sub-sample.

Step 3.4: In a situation where you do not have moisture tester, place the yield in the sacks with proper labels (location, harvesting date, farmer name, village name, etc.). Then, dry the grains to constant weight and record the yield after ambient drying (not oven drying).

Step 4: For all moisture tested samples, convert the grain weight (net harvest area) to 12% moisture content using the following formula (this is done only under conditions, where moisture tester has been used):

1. Introduction

In Egypt, wheat (Triticum aestivum) plays a pivotal role in the country’s agricultural and economic landscape. It is the major component of the national diet and an essential contributor to food security. Its cultivation in the country has a rich history dating back to ancient times. The Nile Delta has always been an ideal location for wheat cultivation. Historically, Egypt was known as the “Breadbasket of the Roman Empire”, highlighting its crucial role in sustaining its population and neighbouring regions. In the country, compared to all crops, it is grown in the largest area (1.33 million ha) and the country produces 9.1 million tons of wheat (average productivity of 6.81 t ha-1) (Source: Economic Affairs Sector, Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, 2023). Compared to all crops, its cultivation area is increasing in the country. However, it is meeting 50% of the demand from the international market to fill the gap between production and consumption (5.86 million t, one of the top 10th largest importers), where the import value of wheat and wheat products was 2.49 billion USD in 2021 (FAOSTAT, 2023).

In recent years (2018-2021), Egypt has shown prominence in reducing imports, where it imported 9.53 million tons wheat in 2021/2022 while it decreased by 17.5% (7.86 million tons) in 2022/2023 (Source: Agriculture Economic Research Institute (AERC). However, to reduce imports sustainably, the country might need to adopt both approaches, i.e., area expansion in New Land and sustainably closing the yield gap in the Old Lands. Adopting science-led demand-driven and sustainable (economic, environmental, and social) farming practices, including improved crop varieties and efficient agronomic management practices, is the key for the sustainable intensification of wheat production in both new and old lands. By implementing below climate-smart wheat production technology tailored to Egypt›s conditions, farmers can enhance their yields, contribute to the country›s demand, and support its agricultural growth.
2. Methodology
2.1 Farmers production practice survey

To understand the existing production practice, attainable yield gaps and major factors determining those yield gaps in wheat cultivation in irrigated dryland system in Egypt, ICARDA has implemented production practice survey in major wheat growing areas covering both old lands and new lands for 2021/22 wheat growing season.

“Old lands"" are the agricultural lands cultivated inside the Nile Valley and the Delta region. It is characterized by clay or silty clay soils, high intensified agriculture system (can be cultivated with 2 or three crops per year), smaller farm holding. ""New lands"" are the agricultural lands reclaimed and cultivated outside the Nile Valley and the Delta region. It is characterized by sandy soils and more frequent salinity problems, a lower intensified agriculture system compared to old lands, more interest in horticulture and high cash crops, and land holding is medium to larger size.

2.2 Yield gap computation

The attainable yield gap was derived based on farmers reported yield from the production practice survey implemented in irrigated drylands in Egypt during 2021 crop growing season. Based on the grain yield, farmers were classified into three categories: top (mean of top 10%), middle (mean of middle 80%), and bottom (mean of bottom 10%). The attainable yield gaps (YG) computed as the difference between the average gain yield of the top 10% of the yield distribution (attainable yield) and the population mean yield.
2.3 Yield gap decomposition

To under the major factors determining the yield variation, the Random Forest (RF) which is a binary tree-based machine-learning method (Breiman, 2001; Cutler et al., 2012) was applied to field- level data on crop management practices, soil, and weather information, which is augmented with household level data on selected socio-economic variables to analyze the major determinants of variations in yield under farmers' management practices for major wheat areas in Egypt. We used the ‘randomForest’ package of the statistical program R (R CoreTeam, 2016) and followed Liaw and Wiener (2002) to set the values of parameters for estimation of the model (mtry = 5, ntree = 1000, and nodesize = 10). 4. Summary

This study analyzed data from 2,042 wheat fields across the major wheat-growing governorates of Egypt, which collectively account for more than 90% of the country's total wheat production. The report synthesizes yield variations and attainable yield gaps in both old lands and Newlands in Egypt and uses a random forests (RF) model to identify the main determinants of these gaps. The findings reveal significant yield gaps of 31% in old lands and 43% in Newlands. In old lands, the most critical factor influencing yield variation was the nitrogen application rate, followed by the application rates of FYM (farmyard manure) and phosphorus, landholding size, soil type, and wheat variety used. In Newlands, the most influential variables were phosphorus application rate, source of irrigation water, number of tillage passes, nitrogen application rate, and seeding method. The variation in yield- determining factors across different governorates suggests that developing and implementing context- specific agronomic solutions can sustainably reduce attainable yield gaps, thereby increasing overall wheat production to meet growing demand in the country.

1. Introduction

Crops yields have been increasing slowly over the past decades despite fast increase in demand. Suitable land and water resources available for crop production are limited in many parts of the world. Increasing crop yields substantially is the best avenue to keep pace with global food demand driven by population and income growth (van Ittersum et al., 2013). To increase productivity on existing land, there is a need to first quantify existing yield gaps followed by decomposing or disaggregating the gap into its components and identify the factors that cause the gap. Data and information on yield gaps and their determinants are important to inform decisions on policy, research, development, and investment that aim to affect future crop yields and land use and decisions and action by individual farmers and farming communities.

The excellence in agronomy (EiA) Initiative aims to deliver agronomic gain at scale for millions of smallholder farming households in prioritized farming systems, with emphasis on supporting women and young farmers, to demonstrate measurable impact on food and nutrition security, income, efficient water use, soil health and climate resilience. EiA delivers agronomic solutions and products in its intervention areas through Use Cases which develop a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) in collaboration with a public or private demand partner that has an active extension network in a target area. The MVP enables the delivery of agronomic product/service at scale to end-users. The design and implementation of MVPs is influenced by data and evidence generated by the Use Cases through the support of teams organized by thematic areas known as Add-ons.

The Add-on themes are designed to inform the initiation, design, piloting, validation, and scaling of MVPs by Use Cases. On of the add-on themes is yield gap decomposition (YGD) which is carried out by a team composed of CGIAR centres participating in the EiA initiative and Advanced Research Institutes (ARIs). Based on available literature and tools, this document presents a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for yield gaps decomposition to be applied to the specific context of EiA Use Cases.

2. Objective of the Yield Gap Decomposition Add-on
The objectives of the YDG add-on are to:
decompose yield gaps into different components,
identify associated major factors that contribute to the gaps, and
influence positively the design and evaluation of the minimum viable products.
3. Framework for the Use of Yield Gaps in Use Cases
A series of steps are required to design, pilot, and scale up the agronomic solution (MVP). These steps are:
(i) due diligence in the identification of a use case,
(ii) use case ideation,
(iii) establish partnership based on demand,
(iv) design the MVP,
(v) decide on the required data and tools,
(vi) develop prototype and get commitment,
(vii) validate the MVP,
(viii) pilot the MVP and
(ix) develop a ready to scale version of the MVP.
Outputs of yield gap decomposition are expected to be used at the following steps of the MVP design and development.
(i) Due diligence- information on yield gaps and yield gap determinates can inform the identification of agronomic problems that can be addressed by developing an agronomic solution.
(ii) Use case ideation- evidence on yield limiting factors that cause yield gaps can be used to prioritize agronomic problems among the many factors that influence productivity of crops.
(iii) Design of MVP – information on yield gaps and the components of yield gaps shall be used to design a clear MVP that can address one or more yield limiting factors.
(iv) Validation of the MVP- knowledge of factors that contribute to yield gaps are useful to evaluate the effectiveness (degree of influence) of the MVP in addressing the major limiting factors.
(v) Scaling the MVP -spatially explicit yield gap decomposition results can be used to identify areas where the MVP is potentially effective and scaled up.

Water-limited potential yield (Yw) refers to the maximum yield that can be obtained under rainfed conditions in a well-defined, and relatively homogeneous, biophysical environment (van Ittersum et al., 2013). Yw can be simulated with crop growth models or derived from perfectly managed rainfed on-station field trials with non-limiting levels of nutrients and no damage from pests, diseases, and weeds.
Actual yield (Ya) refers to the yield of farmers based on their management, and it is recorded from farm surveys or crop cuts.

Attainable yield (Yt): attainable yield also known as exploitable yield is the yield achieved through skillful use of the best available technologies. Some studies use attainable yield as 70 or 80% of either potential yield (irrigated systems) or water limited yield (rainfed systems) (Hall et al., 2013; Ruffo et al., 2013)on individual commercial field (ICF. Yt can be obtained from well managed rainfed on-farm field trials with the best use of available technologies and crop protection measures.
4.2. Yield Gaps

The capacity of a given production system can be evaluated by estimating potential yield and water-limited yield levels as benchmarks for crop production under irrigated and rainfed conditions, respectively. Yield gaps are estimated as the difference between different yield levels such that differences between these potential yield levels and actual farmers’ yields define the yield gaps. The difference between yield potential and average farmers’ yields over a given spatial and temporal scale provides the potential yield gap while the difference between water limited and actual yields provides the water limited or rainfed yield gap (van Ittersum et al., 2013). However, these yield gaps mask intermediate gaps and hence the need to decompose or disaggregate them further.

6. Yield Gap Decomposition Analysis

Yield gap decomposition has been increasingly applied in agronomy to disentangle the impact of sub-optimal management on crop production and to identify agronomic measures to improve yields (Battese & Coelli, 1992; Henderson et al., 2016)Tanzania, Uganda, Ethiopia, Senegal and Burkina Faso. To date, most applications refer to cereal crops (and some tuber and root crops) in a wide range of production systems worldwide, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and Northwest Europe. Different types of yield gap decomposition methods exist such as:
(i) stochastic frontier analysis,
(ii) boundary line analysis, and
(iii) interpretable machine leaning analysis.
6.1. Stochastic Frontier Analysis

The stochastic frontier analysis is the most common of the three methods so far. Besides water-limited potential yield and actual yield described in section 4 above, the frontier yield gap decomposition method considers additional two yield levels (Figure 2) which are defined below.

Highest farmers’ yield (YHF) refers to the maximum yields (e.g., average above the 90th percentile of actual farmers’ yields) observed in a representative sample of farmers sharing similar biophysical conditions (weather and soils) and technologies adopted (e.g., varieties), and

Technical efficient yield (YTEx) refers to the maximum yield that can be achieved by farmers in each environment for a given input level and can be computed using methods of frontier analysis in combination with concepts of production ecology (Silva et al., 2017).

6.2. Boundary Line Analysis

Boundary line analysis has been applied in agronomy to explain yield gaps in farmers’ fields (Webb, 1972). Although there are different approaches for boundary line analysis, the method presented here focuses on the boundary line approach encompassing grouping data and fitting of ‘splines’ to farmer field data. The general features of this approach include (1) identification of boundary points, (2) estimation of a continuous function characterizing the boundary points, and (3) yield gap analysis for each factor and across factors, and the use of the method for yield gap decomposition is described well recently (Wairegi et al., 2010). After estimating boundary lines for individual production factors, von Liebig’s law of the minimum is used to identify the production factor limiting crop yield most. This is done for each field as Ymin = min(Yx1, Yx2, …, Yxn), where Yxn is the yield predicted with the boundary line for a given production factor. Estimation of Ymin allows identifying the limiting factor to crop yield and decomposing the yield gap into an ‘identified yield gap’ (IYG) and an ‘unexplained yield gap’ (UYG) in each field. IYG is defined as the difference between the water- limited yield and the Ymin. UYG is defined as the difference between Ymin and the reported actual yield.
An example of yield gap decomposition analysis using boundary line analysis based on cassava dada is presented HERE.

The case study shows clear boundary lines between cassava yield and growing season rainfall, soil fertility, soil texture, and pest, disease and weed management practices, which were identified as the key constraints to cassava production in East Africa (Fermont et al., 2009).
Interpretable Machine Learning

Machine learning lies at the intersection of computer science and statistics and has been used to unravel patterns in large datasets that are challenging to analyze with more conventional statistical approaches. Machine learning is increasingly being used in agriculture to predict crop yield. There are different types of machine learning methods which can be identified based on their interpretability and level of complexity as: (i) regression-based methods (e.g., linear, ridge, and lasso regression), (ii) single tree- or multiple tree- based methods (e.g., classification and regression trees, gradient boosting, extreme gradient boosting, and random forest), and (iii) decision boundary-based support vector regression.

Regression-based methods are parametric, and their coefficients are obtained through ordinary least-squares. Tree-based methods such as classification and regression tree, random forest, and gradient boosting rely on decision trees, and a series of if-then rules to arrive at a particular prediction or classification. Distance-based methods, like K-nearest mean, find the K-nearest neighbors in the feature space and provide predictions based on those K data point’s outcomes. Decision boundary-based methods create a decision boundary with data projected in a higher dimension (suppose there are three variables, then their values will be projected in a 3-dimensional space) to derive a particular prediction. Regression-based methods are less complex and have easier and more direct interpretation compared to tree-based or distance and decision boundary-based methods.

Some of the methods mentioned above have been used in agronomy research over the recent years, and their performance has been compared (Nayak et al., 2022). The most important feature of machine learning for yield gap decomposition is the estimation of shapely values from a tuned random forest model. The Shapely additive explanation technique ranks individual variables and identifies the yield contribution of each variable as deviations from mean predicted yield by the model.

7. Application of Yield Gap Decomposition Information by the
Use Cases

Information on yield gaps and the different components of the gap (technology, resource, and efficiency) are important for EiA Use Cases to get answers for critical questions that may arise at different levels of the MVP development process. Based on then framework described in section 3, the main questions that can be raised and answered by yield gap decomposition evidence during the MVP development processes are summarized in Box 1.
Box 1. Importance of yield gap decomposition for use case development

(i) Due diligence- What are the yield limiting factors in the area? Information on yield gaps and yield gap determinates can inform the identification of agronomic problems that can be addressed by developing an agronomic solution. (ii) Use case ideation- What are the most important yield liming factors in the area? Evidence on yield limiting factors that cause yield gaps can be used to prioritize agronomic problems among the many factors that influence productivity of crops. (iii) Design of MVP — How much is the level of productivity increase that can be achieved through a use case? Information on yield gaps and the components of yield gaps shall be used to design a measurable MVP that can address one or more yield limiting factors. (iv) Validation of the MVP- How much is the productivity increase achieved by the intervention (s) of the use case? Knowledge of factors that contribute to yield gaps are useful to evaluate the effectiveness (degree of influence) of the MVP is addressing the major limiting factors. (v) Scaling the MVP — Which areas have the same yield limiting problems addressed by the use cases? Spatially explicit yield gap decomposition results can be used to identify areas where the MVP is potentially effective and scaled up.

In general, yield gap decomposition results are useful to develop measurable MVP and monitor and track agronomic gain along the MVP steps. Decomposed yield gaps can also be used to generate lessons that can be used in feedback loops to further improve the MVP and scaling it. The lessons and agronomic gains can be obtained from well deigned baseline and endline surveys (digitally or in person) or continuous measurements from on-farm measurements.

INTRODUCTION
Survey Objectives

The Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) initiative aims to deliver agronomic gain for millions of smallholder farming households, with emphasis on women and young farmers for measurable impact on food and nutrition security, income, water use, soil health, and climate resilience. This objective will be achieved through:
• Facilitating the delivery of agronomic solutions, including co-creation and deployment of gender- and youth-responsive solutions to smallholder farmers via scaling partners.

• Enabling the creation of value from big data and advanced analytics, through the assembly and governance of data and tools; application of existing analytics and solutions for specific use cases; supply of information on climate impacts, inclusivity, and sustainability of agronomic solutions; and national agricultural research system (NARS) capacity strengthening.
• Driving the next generation of agronomy at scale innovations by addressing key knowledge gaps and facilitating innovation in agronomy research through engagement with partners.

• Nurturing internal efficiencies for an agile and demand-driven agronomy research and development community through internal organization and external partnerships prioritization, demand mapping, and foresight. for

A survey tool was developed by the EiA add-on teams for administering by Use Case teams within their place of work. The tool was developed to understand farmer segmentation, gender and generational differences in agricultural management practices and technology adoption, yield gap decomposition and key performance indicators of agronomic gains, and current practices in the Use Case population of interest. With this better understanding, along with an understanding of other contextual factors, Use Case teams will have the necessary information to inform the design of their Minimum Viable Products (MVPs) to ensure they meet the needs of women, men, youth, and different farmer types and help increase yields and other agronomic gain outcomes.
Sample

The sample must represent the primary population who will be targeted by the MVP – within the country or region of the country where the Use Case is implementing its research. Hence, for EiA, these are farm households who grow at least one of the focal crops of the Use Case, in the geographical area where the Use Case intends to reach farmers during the validation and piloting stages of the MVP. The sample strategy will be outlined in a separate document, but we highlight the important components relevant to the enumerators here.

Critical to a good household survey is the definition of a household and who would be considered a household member (see Box 1). We propose a standard definition here, though the Use Case teams can propose a modification depending on their context and commonly used definitions in national household surveys for their country.
Box 1. Household and household member definition
The concept of household is based on the arrangements made by persons, individually or in groups, for providing themselves with food or other essentials for living. A household may be either:
a) A one-person household: a person who makes provision for his or her own food or other essentials for living without combining with any other person to form part of a multi-person household, or

b) A multi-person household: a group of two or more persons living together who make common provision for food or other essentials for living. The persons in the group may pool their resources and may have a common budget. They may be related or unrelated persons, or constitute a combination of persons both related and unrelated. If someone stays in the same household but does not bear any costs for food or does not take food from the same pot, they are not considered household members.
Importantly, a person is only considered a household member if s/he was present in the household for at least 6 months in the past 12 months and for at least half of the weeks in these months.
Exceptions include:
- Permanent joiners: people who recently joined the household with the intention of permanently staying in the household, for example, after childbirth, marriage or other.
- Permanent leavers: people who recently left the household and who do not intend to rejoin the household in the near future. For example, people who passed away, who left for marriage, etc.
- Children who are away more than 6 months of the year for educational purposes.

The survey must also represent male and female primary decision makers within farm households (see Box 2). If a household does not consist of an adult male household member, only one female primary decision maker can be interviewed. Likewise, if there is no adult female household member in a household then only one male primary decision maker can be interviewed.
Box 2. Definition of primary male and female decision makers
The primary respondent should be either the man or woman in the household who is targeted by the Use Case, or in the case of a control group, the “type” of man or woman targeted by the Use Case.

The other primary respondent is typically the spouse of the primary respondent, or if the spouse is not available, another adult household member of the opposite sex who is primarily responsible for making both social and economic decisions related to agriculture.

If multiple eligible adults are present, the main choice should be the person (either male or female) who is cultivating the Use Case focal crop and who is the main decision maker regarding the agronomic practices applied to the Use Case focal crop.

The primary and secondary respondents are usually husband and wife in a dual-headed household, however, they can also be another member as long as there is one male and one female aged 18 and over. For instance, a woman could be living with her adult son/daughter or a man could be living with an adult daughter/son. The first choice should be to interview the main decision maker of issues related to the Use Case focal crop and their spouse. Another respondent should only be interviewed if the spouse is not available.

It may also be the case that there is only a primary female respondent and there is no adult male present in the household, or that there is only a primary male respondent but no adult female respondent. In this case only one person, the primary decision maker for the Use Case focal crop, will be interviewed.
In case the primary decision maker for the Use Case focal Crop is a polygamous male respondent, one wife should be randomly selected to be interviewed.
Survey Modules

There are two parts to the gender-youth assessment survey, identified as Part 1 and Part 2 (Box 3). Part 1 includes the main household questionnaire; whereas Part 2 consists of the individual questionnaire. The household questionnaire asks general questions regarding the household. This part can be answered by any knowledgeable household member, as well as by multiple household members. The household questionnaire offers information on the households’ socio-economic status, including household composition and farm practices.

The individual questionnaire should be administered to one male and one female primary decision maker in the household, as identified in the household questionnaire. This questionnaire contains questions pertaining to the individual who responds to the questionnaire. To ensure that the respondent answers freely, the enumerator should ensure the respondent is interviewed separately. No other household members or other should be present or able to overhear the interview, except for small children below two years of age.

Household Information Sheet
Privacy and Confidentiality

To ensure privacy, enumerators are not allowed to interview anyone they know. If you are assigned a household where you know someone, you should inform your team leader. The team leader will re-assign that household to another enumeration team, and your team will be assigned a different household.

All data collected by you for this survey will be completely confidential. These data should not be discussed with anyone other than with your team leader. You should not share information from the survey -- including the names of respondents (the individuals who are interviewed) – with anyone. Even within a household, you should not show responses provided by one member to any other member of the household.

Data from several thousand respondents will be consolidated for reports. Respondents’ names will not be reported, and it will not be possible for anyone to deduce the identity of respondents from the reports.
Enumerator’s Role

The enumerator is pivotal to the success of the survey. Close adherence to procedures for conducting the interviews and entering data will ensure the quality of the survey. The enumerator’s responsibilities include:
• Participating in the household listing.
• Locating the assigned households and completing Module A, Household Information Sheet, for each household.
• Explaining the survey to the household and obtaining signed informed consent to participate in the survey, as in Module B.
• Identifying all members of the household who are eligible to be interviewed for each of the survey modules.
• Interviewing all eligible members for all modules, including returning to the household if eligible members were absent on the first visit.
• Entering the respondent’s answers onto the tablet accurately.
• Submitting the interview data to the team leader and discussing issues with the team leader; and
• Tracking and reporting progress in completing assignments.
• Documenting challenges encountered during field data collection.
Detailed instructions on how to complete these tasks are provided in this manual.
CONDUCTING THE INTERVIEW
General Guidance

The enumerator represents the Excellence in Agronomy Initiative and <survey implementer> to the households assigned to the enumeration team. The enumerator needs to make a favorable impression on household members. Enumerators should follow these basic guidelines:
• Dress appropriately for fieldwork (according to the culture of the place of assignment).
• Address all community and household members encountered politely and with respect.

• Visit households during appropriate hours. (Note: enumerators may need to visit a household outside these hours to interview someone who was not available during the initial visit. This will be planned with the household.)
• Treat all information that you collect as strictly confidential.
Introduction in the Household

As a potential stranger in the house, it is important to observe all the rules and customs governing visits to other people’s houses. Please follow these steps at the beginning of each household visit:
• Knock first and greet everyone
Introduce yourself politely and say that you are working for <survey implementer>
• Ask to speak with a head of the household.
• Explain that you are there to conduct a survey on farming practices and that local authorities have approved the survey.
• Ask permission to enter the house if appropriate.
• You should automatically show your <some proof of legitimacy as enumerator> in all cases.

Be patient with household residents who appear suspicious of the interview. Carefully explain the purpose of the interview, the fact that all information is completely confidential, and the fact that respondents can refuse to respond to any question.
Ensuring Privacy

Make sure that only household members are present during the administration of the main household questionnaire (Part 1). Friends, neighbors, or other non-household members should not be present during the household interview.

For Part 2 especially, which raises many questions about gender, personal opinions, and decision-making that cannot be answered truthfully with other adults around, respondents should be interviewed separately from other household members. Make sure that only the person who is the main respondent to a survey module is present during the enumeration of that module. Although there may be situations where it will be difficult to separate a respondent from his or her family due to different reasons (e.g. care activities, social norms …) you should aim to have only the principal respondent to the module present. If it is unavoidable to have children around, it is okay for them to remain, but other adults should not be present. Further, you should pay special attention to avoiding having other adult household members around. In case local customs and norms mandate that respondents and interviewers are of the same gender, the teams should organize themselves to accommodate these customs.
Asking Questions
There are many procedures you should follow to ensure a high-quality interview:
• Do not rush the interview. Allow the respondent time to think before responding. Let the respondent know that his/her answer is very important.

• Read the question exactly as it is written (or as you were taught to translate it during training). Read it slowly and clearly. If the respondent does not understand the question, explain what the question is asking, and then reread the question slowly.

• Unless instructed to do so, do not read the list of possible answers to the respondent. Let the respondent answer on his/her own. You then select the survey response that best matches the answer given by the respondent.
• Do not suggest responses.
• Remain neutral. Do not give the impression that any response is more appropriate than others. Never appear to disapprove of any response.
• Respondents may have multiple responses to a given question. If the questions allow only one answer, you should enter the response that the respondent says is true most of the time.

• Respondents may provide long answers that include a lot of information not directly relevant to the question. Simply record the relevant response and ignore non-pertinent information. If the respondent has not answered the question at all, steer the respondent politely back to the question.
• Do not argue with respondents.

• If the respondent is reluctant to answer a question, explain that individual responses will be completely confidential, and that it is normal to not always know the right answer, but that having their best guess will be incredibly helpful. If the respondent still will not answer the question, select ‘refused’ and proceed to the next question.
Interviewing Instructions on the Questionnaire and Tablet

You will be conducting the interview from a tablet. When reading questions from the tablet, please phrase them as it appears. Pay attention to special instructions that are not to be read to the respondent or questions containing blanks that you will need to fill in as you speak. For example, please do not read “NAME” in the following question: “How old is [NAME]?” Rather, read the actual name of the relevant household member.
Reporting Issues to the Team Leader

For many questions, the enumerator must interpret the respondent’s answer. Sometimes this may be difficult. Write down the household ID, respondent, question number, and anything that you want to discuss with your team leader. It will be possible to change a response after discussing it with the team leader following the interview. You should keep such notes organized so that you do not confuse households, respondents, modules, or questions with one another.
Please alert your team leader of any problems regarding the tablet survey immediately.
FIELDWORK PROCEDURES
Enumeration Team

Typically enumeration teams work with a fixed set of enumerators which are responding to one supervisor. Typically, teams consist of about 4-5 enumerators for one supervisor. The exact number however can differ depending on the specific context and logistics. Each enumerator will have his/her tablet for entering data. Each enumeration team member is responsible for his/her tablet. If you must exchange tablets with your enumeration team partner because your tablet’s battery is too low or for any other reason, note this on the control sheet. Also, note that the team leader will collect your tablet every evening to review and save data and recharge your tablet. Make sure the team leader always returns the correct tablet to you. Enumerators are expected to stick to this rule because it is very essential for the success of any survey.
Control Sheet

Members of the enumeration team will be given a control sheet that lists all households assigned to the team in that cluster (see Annex A). The control sheet will provide the household number that will be used on the survey forms. 1. Introduction

This report serves as a youth and gender diagnostic assessment for the DRC-OLAM-Coffee Use Case in the Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) Initiative. This Use Case focuses on Organic coffee-based systems. Following the request of the “Demand partner”, the decision support tools (DSTs) for organic coffee will be combined with advice on agronomic practices of coffee or coffee farmer typologies to ensure the tool meets farmers’ requirements. According to Olam food ingredients (Ofi), the “Demand partner” under this Use Case, farmers are diverse and they probably do not need the same supports (agricultural inputs, trainings, etc.) to improve the productivity and resilience of coffee-based system, farmers’ income, and livelihoods. According to Lambrecht et al. (2023), agronomic solutions are key for improving yields, farm incomes and food security; and digital tools and extension services are promising options to deliver such optimized agronomic solutions at scale. However, in many different settings female farmers have less access to agricultural extension services and on average significantly lower agricultural productivity on their fields compared to male-owned or jointly owned fields (Aguilar et al., 2015; Ghebru and Holden, 2015; Bezabih et al., 2016). The OLAM-Coffee Use Case needed an improved understanding on how the developed tool will be useful for men and women farmers as well as for the younger and the older generations. The results presented in this study report will be instrumental in the scaling and dissemination phases of the Use Case.

The descriptive analysis of this study follows the steps of the Reach-Benefit-Empower-Transform framework of Quisumbing, Meinzen-Dick and Malapit (2021). This framework highlights that reaching women and youth with agronomic solutions and associated extension approaches requires including them in project activities (Quisumbing et al., 2023; Lambrecht et al., 2023). Thus, aligning the diagnostic assessment under OLAM-Coffee Use Case with this framework helps to ensure that we appropriately anticipate gender and youth dynamics that may occur in each step of the framework. The diagnostic tool can then serve to inform the design (or re design) of the minimum viable products (MVPs) and associated extension approaches to be validated and piloted by this Use Cases in DRC.
2. Data collection and Methodology
2.1 Data collection

Data were collected in September and October 2023 in two territories of South Kivu province in the Eastern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) (Figure 1). These territories include Kabare and Kalehe which were selected based on the importance of coffee production, coffee being the target crop of “OLAM Coffee Use Case” and also on the operational areas (mandate areas) of the Virunga Coffee in South Kivu province. Virunga Coffee is a private operator and main coffee exporter in the country but also the demand partner under the OLAM Coffee Use Case in DRC.

A list of coffee farmers belonging to coffee cooperatives working with Virunga Coffee in both Kabare and Kalehe was provided by the Virunga coffee team for selection of households to be interviewed. The presented list contained information on household identification and composition, coffee field area, planted coffee varieties, number of coffee trees per field, coffee yield per field among others. In order to have a representative sample of coffee farmers in the study area, households were grouped in four classes based on two criteria: the size of the coffee field and the coffee yield per field (or number of coffee trees per field). The first class comprised households with large coffee field and high yield; the second class contained households with large coffee field but low yield, the third class contained households with small coffee field and high yield while the fourth class included farmers with a small coffee field and low yield.

Prior to the survey, 63 households were randomly selected in each class, giving a total of 250 coffee farmers per territory. A back up list of coffee farmers in each class and territory was kept and used when households of the first selected list were not available. In total, 500 different households were interviewed. Involvement of women in coffee crop cultivation was a criterion used for selection of households in each class.

2.2 Statistical analysis

Data collected at household, individual, and plot levels were analysed using R 4.4.1 software (R core team, 2024), enabling a multi-level statistical approach that offered a comprehensive understanding of disparities and patterns across the Kabare and Kalehe territories. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the key demographic and agronomic variables, including household size, the composition of male and female members, youth presence, cultivated area, and respondent characteristics such as age, marital status, education, and literacy. Distributions were presented in frequency tables, means, and percentages to provide an initial overview of data structure and territorial differences. Chi-square test was used to evaluate the associations between territories, gender-based variables, and food insecurity prevalence, identifying statistically significant differences where applicable. Additionally, attitudes and social norms regarding gender equality were analyzed through responses to relevant statements. Statistical significance was determined at thresholds of p < 0.05, 0.01, and 0.001. To enhance clarity and accessibility, the analyses incorporated graphical presentations such as bar charts and cross-tabulations, highlighting findings related to sources of agricultural advice, mobile device ownership, and access to financial services. Gender and youth dynamics in decision-making and agronomic preferences were visually represented to identify disparities and intervention opportunities.
3. Results
3.1 Household and respondent characteristics

The surveyed households have on average 7.8 members in both Kabare and Kalehe (Table 2). The average household size in Kalehe is larger with 8.53 members than in Kabare with 7.16 members, and households in the former territory are more likely to include children under five than the later territory (67.87 % in Kalehe vs. 42.63 % in Kabare). Most households (80 %) have both male and female adults, whereas 1 % of the population include male adults only, and 1 % consists of female adults only. Both Kabare and Kalehe have a high proportion of households with youth members (79.4 %), though male youth presence is higher in Kabare, while female youth presence is slightly more common in Kalehe. On average, the household head is 54 years old, and only 1.6 % of household heads are youth.

Given the nature of the study topic, all households in our sample are coffee farm households. On average, a household cultivates 2.7 different plots on 2.4 hectares. However, households in Kalehe cultivate more plots in average, yet Kabare households tend to manage a slightly larger total area (Table 2).

However, youth display a much higher percentage of single individuals (51.6 %) compared to non-youth respondents (2.6 %).

Male respondents are more educated than female respondents: 77.3 % of the male respondents versus 42.7 % of female respondents have received at least primary school education, and 22.3 % of the male respondents versus 55.8 % of female respondents are literate. Religion is largely Catholic and Protestant for both groups, with no significant differences. Ethnicity shows a predominance of Shi and Havu across all groups, though youth are less represented among Shi compared to non-youth.

Poverty and food insecurity are high among the surveyed households. Majority of the households (96.6 %) moderate or severe food insecure (Table 4), with this proportion slightly higher in Kalehe (98.8 %) than in Kabare (94.4 %). As shown in Figure 2, most of the households (94 %) reported skipping meals or being unable to access healthy and nutritious food during the last 12 months, indicating a lack of quality food and accessibility. Moreover, 92 % of the respondents indicated that they ate only a limited variety of foods and are worried about food scarcity, revealing both limited dietary diversity and widespread anxiety about food availability. Furthermore, 87 % of the households reported having eaten less than they felt necessary while 86 % ran out of food during the last 12 months, indicating food shortages at the household level. While less common, severe hunger was reported as 83 % of the responded indicated that they felt hungry without being able to eat, and 25% went a full day without food during the last 12 months. These findings underscore a pervasive and urgent food insecurity problem, characterized by limited access, reduced dietary diversity, and constant food-related stress. Only a small fraction of surveyed households (2.8 %) is food secure, with a higher food security in Kabare (4.78 %) compared to Kalehe (0.80 %). Mild food insecurity is rare, affecting less than 1% in
each territory. This result indicates that food insecurity is a substantial issue across the surveyed households in the study area.

3.2. Women and youth’s contribution to agricultural production

Both men and women work in agriculture in the study sites, although men are involved to a larger extent than women. Data presented were collected on all household members by household (Table 5) and by all plots cultivated by each household (Table 6). Considering all household members, in 65% of households both male and female household members are actively involved in crop production, while in 30.4% of households only male household members are actively farming (Table 5). It is rare to find households with only female (and no male) household members involved in crop farming (only 4.6% of households). Overall, 65% of households have female members actively involved in farming and 51.2% of plots have female members actively working on them (Table 5 and 6).

Women have decision-making power on the farm in only 4.6% of households and in 16.6% of plots, with men still considered the main decision-makers to farm work (in 65% of households and in 32.3% of plots). Both youth and non-youth members are actively involved in farming (in 80.8% of households and 80.6% of plots). However, youth are rarely considered as main decision maker if other non-youth household members are also involved in farming. Only 4.2% of plots are managed mainly by youth. Non-youth household members are considered the main decision maker in 88.4% of households and on 95.8% of plots (Tables 5 and 6).

3.3 Reaching women and youth

Most of male and female respondents (99 percent) report having access to agricultural advice or extension services in the past 12 months. However, much of this advice is obtained from the private sectors (54 % for men and 49 % for women) and farmer associations (21 % for men and 18 % for women) for both men and women (Figure 3), and much less of this advice is from professional service providers such as government extension services, traders and input dealers, radio or social media (jointly, they reach only 13.4 % of male respondent and 15.8 % of female respondents). This demonstrates the importance of social network in the study area and the reliance on the formal institutions, especially the private sectors, but it also points out the scarcity of the professional extension services for both men and women.

Overall, female youth seem most deprived of professional extension advice, and rely to the largest extent on private extension services for advice (73 %) as compared to any other respondents (Figure 4). Female non-youth do get more advice from farmer associations, relatives, government extension services or traders. Social media and radio are rarely used across all groups, indicating a general preference for more direct, traditional sources of extension information.
